#4087. Sony Seemingly Winding Down PSVR2 Sales, Gone from USA Store

Sony may be taking steps to wind down sales of its PSVR2 headset, as it's been spotted that the VR device is no longer being sold through some of its official regional outlets and at third-party retailers.

For a few weeks now, fans have been picking up on the fact PSVR2 no longer appears on the official PlayStation Direct website in the USA. I did a search of the website today, and the headset is nowhere to be seen.

If you scroll down the PS5 accessories tab on the USA webpage, you'll find a PSVR2 heading, but the actual device isn't there. You only receive options to purchase the charging station, the PC adapter, and a third-party case:

Besides these examples within the PSVR2 tab, I can find absolutely no evidence the VR device exists on the PlayStation Direct site for USA customers. For now, at least, the PSVR2 headset is still for sale on the UK side of PlayStation Direct.

The situation goes further, though, according to Road to VR, which has done a deep dive into regional data relating to PSVR2. According to them, the removal of the headset from regional PlayStation Direct pages began in mid-October, which is when fans started noticing it was gone. The link that should have taken you to the PSVR2 purchase page was producing a 404 error.

As the outlet also highlights, retailers like Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart do have stock listed, but it comes from third-party retailers at considerable markups over the normal price of the headset — around $750 at Best Buy.

It appears more difficult than ever to buy a PSVR2 at its recommended retail price.

News Sony Seemingly Ends VR Ambitions by Selling Patents to Meta

To get a better gauge on what's happening, it'll be interesting to see if any PSVR2 discounts are revealed around Black Friday. Last year, Sony knocked $100 off the price for the spending period. It'll be interesting to see if anything happens this month — and if there's even stock to facilitate a discount.

Of course, PlayStation's first-party support for PSVR2 has been woeful. Third-parties have brought their games to the VR platform, but Sony called it a day on launch, after Horizon Call of the Mountain, in terms of dedicated PSVR2 titles. Most recently, it sold its VR patents to Meta, which hammered another nail into any VR efforts from Sony in the future.

Ahsoka star Eman Esfandi suggests more animated characters could make the leap to live-action in season 2

Esfandi, who plays Ezra Bridger, also confirmed we're getting a "lot of Chopper" in Ahsoka season 2 during an appearance alongside co-stars Rosario Dawson and Natasha Liu Bordizzo at L.A. The Star Wars series, of course, has already brought over plenty of familiar animated names to live-action – including Ahsoka herself, Grand Admiral Thrawn, Ezra Bridger, Sabine Wren, Hera, and even slightly deeper cuts such as the David Tennant-voiced droid Huyang.

The first season of Ahsoka also carried on much of Thrawn's storyline that punctuated much of the third and fourth seasons of Star Wars: Rebels. The first Ahsoka season 2 trailer also teased that we'll be hurtling back to the Clone Wars era for a series of scenes between Hayden Christensen's Anakin Skywalker and Ahsoka, AKA 'Snips'.

But Ahsoka won't just be concerned about the past. Rosario Dawson also suggested on the same panel that the Disney Plus show should pose some intriguing questions for the future, too.

Dawson said, “I think especially the way the series… how it comes together… I think the direction we end up going in leads to some really interesting questions and ideas about what the future holds."

Ahsoka season hits Disney Plus from January 20. For more, check out the upcoming Star Wars movies in the works beyond that.

#4085. Mass Effect 5 was named Universe partly because it let players generate alternate timelines based on their choices in previous entries, technical director says

The system was part of BioWare's effort to give the player "absolute autonomy", according to Romain Toutain

In case you missed it, an internal trailer for the new Mass Effect game which BioWare were working on prior to EA shutting them down hit the net late last week. It offered a peek at what the studio were cooking with this new entry, dubbed Mass Effect Universe. According to its technical director, one of the reasons the game was given that name was that it had a system aimed at letting players form alternate timelines based on their choices in previous Mass Effects.

Romain Toutain, BioWare's franchise technical director since 2022, said as much during a Twitch stream that saw him react to the leaked trailer. The on-demand version of this steam looks like it may since have been yanked, but not before a BlueSky user with the handle @loustica-lucia went through, took some clips, and added subtitles translating Toutain as he chats about the trailer in French.

"All the choices made in the first Mass Effect games were taken into account," the developer said after the trailer finished. "One of the reasons why it was called Mass Effect Universe is that you had so many choices that you could plug your saves together to create parallel universes. To keep it simple. It’s not exactly how it worked. You had different timelines, basically. You could almost generate timelines, kinda like Zero Time [Dilemma]."

So earlier, my brother was watching Octobinz (Romain Toutain)'s livestream on Twitch. He was the Technical Director on Mass Effect Universe, so I wanted to share some bits he discussed. As he speaks french, I added subtitles to make it more accessible for everyone! #MassEffect #MassEffectUniverse[image or embed]

Asked if it was similar to Dragon Age Keep, the service BioWare set up to let folks create world states based on their Dragon Age: Origins and Dragon Age 2 choices that they could then import into Inquisition, Toutain said "kinda". Though, he stressed that this Mass Effect system worked in some extra complexity by letting players make decisions that might contradict things they've previously done.

"Everything in the game, everything was stateful," the dev explained. "At any time, you could stop the game - I mean, you could pause it - and ask a system that solved logical equations, ‘Is this valid?’ And if it isn’t valid, what conditions must be met for it to be valid? For the game to set these conditions. And if the content doesn’t exist, then we know the content doesn’t exist, so we’ll either have to create another branch, either that, or we know we have to create the content.

"So, if you killed a guy, and you needed that guy for your mission, the game will make sure you can complete the mission. Or, if that’s what the designers have decided, well, no, the mission’s failed because you killed that guy. Or else, something that was bound to happen doesn’t happen, just so that a path remains open, so that you can get around the problem." Toutain summed the system up as being something that was "difficult to set up", but worked well.

It certainly sounds ambitious, if a lot of work to get right. Whether it and the pursuit of giving the player "absolute autonomy" which the dev says it was part of would've made Mass Effect 5 a return to form for BioWare is up for debate and will likely remain so forever unless someone swoops in to perform a miracle resurrection pretty sharpish. Personally, it at least sounds like something that'd have piqued my curiosity enough to see what Shep and co were up to, despite not being the biggest Mass Effecter.

#4084. South Of Midnight Director Reflects On Why He Was 'Always Worried' About Funding At Xbox

"It just seems like, in hindsight at least, it was unsustainable."

We absolutely loved South of Midnight when it launched last year as an Xbox first-party title from Compulsion Games, and it's still one of our favourite Xbox Game Studios releases of recent years. However, a year later, Xbox has parted ways with the development team and helped transition them back to an independent studio.

In a nutshell, it seems Xbox wasn't happy enough with South of Midnight's performance from a revenue standpoint, and the same could be said for other smaller releases last year like Double Fine's Keeper and Kiln.

Some fans had been voicing their concerns prior to these releases that Xbox might be putting too much funding into them, and speaking on a recent podcast, South of Midnight director David Sears admitted that he was "always worried" that the funding situation might change and cause Xbox to "close the floodgates".

Here's an excerpt from the MinnMax podcast in which he said this:

"I mean, [Xbox] were funding a lot of games. They were also funding a lot of studios that, you know, I was like, well, okay, great. I guess you have infinite money. Like I was saying earlier, I don't want to feel the weight of the obligation of giant budget or an army of 600 to be responsible for. I want to make something that isn't going to bankrupt Microsoft, I guess, or the games division."

"So, you know, on one hand, if everyone you're working with is either trying to make generational games at not a huge expense, or games that have huge or really significant contemporary commercial appeal, great. It's going to work. But when does that ever happen?"

"I literally told people, 'Wow, this could be terrible.' Because somebody is going to say one day, 'We're closing those floodgates.' And that's going to have really traumatic results downstream."

Perhaps most shockingly, the director went on to admit that as much as he wanted to make South of Midnight, it perhaps wasn't sustainable from a funding perspective in hindsight, and that a "shocking outcome" seemed inevitable.

"I mean, I wanted to make it. No doubt, and obviously, because we made it. Would I have turned off someone else's money flow before South of Midnight? Yeah, 'cause I'm not completely selfless. But it just seems like, in hindsight at least, it was unsustainable. So, of course it was going to have a shocking outcome."

"I mean, it's easy to dissect it now. At the time, I would talk to other directors and would be like, 'How is this happening? How did we get so lucky? Is this a golden era?' And I would always be like, 'For now, right? There's always a night when Rome burns.' And I didn't know exactly when it would be, but I was always worried about it."

Of course, none of this is to suggest that Sears wasn't proud of South of Midnight, or that he didn't think it was worthwhile, but it just appears he was concerned with the Xbox money was putting into (and expecting back) for it.

Nevertheless, it seems like he had a very positive experience working with Microsoft overall:

"To their credit, it's amazing, right? I think there's definitely corporate Microsoft DNA but they're vastly different from the Microsoft I knew back in the '90s or the early 2000s, right? Much more humane, actually. It's remarkable and commendable."

"Working on South of Midnight, it became clear to me - some games, their time is not on release. Some games are generational, right? Something that has a good message or is transportive to places that will remain timeless will endure and audiences will find them."

His prediction did ultimately come true - Xbox decided to "close the floodgates" earlier this year by splitting from multiple studios including Compulsion Games, and seemingly adopting a new strategy of focusing on their core franchises like Halo, Forza, Gears, Fallout and others.

We're just pleased that Compulsion Games didn't end up getting closed altogether, and that South of Midnight did actually see the light of day instead of being cancelled during development. We reckon it could end up being one of those Sunset Overdrive-style titles in the future - a cult classic that people end up really enjoying from years past.

#4083. GTA 6 PS5 File Size Confirmed to Be 212GB, Physical Map Available But Not in Boxed Copies

Rockstar Games has today shared more details on the launch of GTA 6, across both its digital and physical versions on PS5.

Rumoured last week via a social media account, it has now been confirmed that GTA 6 requires 212GB of space to be downloaded and installed. You'll be able to preload the game, and that option has actually been brought forward by two days.

GTA 6 preload will now be available from Tuesday, 10th November 2026. The title then releases for PS5 and Xbox Series X|S on 19th November 2026.

Further, a mainstay of past GTA physical editions, a map of the game world will be produced — but it won't come with the physical "code in a box" editions. Instead, it'll be purchasable for $0.99 from the official Rockstar Store, or bundled in for free with any purchase you make from the storefront — that's if you want a real physical version of it.

Alternatively, there'll be a digital download of the GTA 6 boxart and the Leonida map, which I suppose you could just print out yourself.

#4082. 32-year-old "ellipsoid" horror game Ecstatica gets a PC re-release today, showing us an alternative timeline in which polygonal 3D never became dominant

One of my favourite hobbies is digging up older pieces of gaming tech or software know-how and asking myself: "man, what would the world have been like, if every GPU were made out of Gorgonzola?" Or less silly words to that effect. Nostalgia aside, it's useful to revisit historical alternatives in the face of very rich people who would have us believe that only their trillion-dollar boondoggle is "the" future.

The code running 1994 horror game Ecstatica probably isn't going to topple Unreal Engine anytime soon, but look at this article's header image, and tell me you aren't fascinated. Why is everything so… pert? I will tell you why: Ecstatica's graphics make heavy use of ellipsoids. They're the basis for everything from werewolf buttocks to the grain of castle flagstones. You can experience this terrifying bubble-wrap reality for yourself in today's Steam and GOG re-release of both Ecstatica and its sequel, care of SNEG Games.

I myself know about Ecstatica thanks to Jasper Byrne, developer of the brilliant Lone Survivor, whom I spoke to yonks ago about "de-making" and monolithic progress narratives. Byrne mentioned it as an example of a road-not-taken in videogame graphics production and aesthetics. Or at least, a road-not-taken-very-far.

Created by Andrew Spencer Studios, Ecstatica uses ellipsoids with actual volumes for characters, most objects, and much of the environment - all of it running on the CPU. It schlops and schlurps the ellipsoids together into more complex, rounded masses. Look at the slightly nauseating ovoid grit of those dungeon walls. It's like somebody wallpapered their kid's bedroom with xenomorph eggs. Ugh, I'm getting Yedoma Globula flashbacks.

As such, Ecstatica cuts against what would become the dominant trend of using polygons for 3D visuals, though the game's engine is capable of rendering polygons for square or flat objects such as doors and crosses. As for what you actually do, in this appallingly bulbous simulation: you are an unfortunate wanderer who's strayed into a village full of monsters. There are many ways to die. Released two years before the original Resident Evil, Ecstatica is an early example of fixed-perspective survival horror, splintering off from adventure games. It's puzzle-driven with a lot of "absurd British humour", as the Steam and GOG storepages for the re-release explain.

I'm not sure who exactly worked on this port, but publishers SNEG were founded in 2020 by former GOG staffers, with the goal of restoring or, at least, republishing and resurfacing various forgotten PC games. The Ecstatica rebuild includes controller support and three graphics modes, changeable on the fly: one for the original DOS version of the game, one for the 1997 re-release on Windows 95, and a "real-time high resolution render". I'm not sure if any of the original devs are involved - they broke up after Ecstatica 2, midway through development of their third game Urban Decay. The latter was also ellipsoid-based, but the devs switched to a more familiar polygonal look before the project ran out of gas.

#4080. Clean a whole planet with a toothbrush in Moon Sweepers, the PowerWash genre's latest crime against perfectionists

I don't much go for PowerWash Simulator-likes, but there is something appealingly unwholesome about a game in which you have to wipe the dust off an entire moon. Using a toothbrush. True, you can upgrade to beefier hoovering equipment in Moon Sweepers by cashing in shipments of lunar dirt, but that strikes me as a dangerous concession to brute mass production thinking – it risks consigning centuries of artisanal knowledge to, well, the dustbin.

Take pride in your craft, colleagues! If we become over-reliant on hoover-me-dos, we'll lose the skill of cleansing celestial objects by hand, and sooner or later, they'll give our jobs to the bots. You can keep your new-fangled vacuum mops. If anybody needs me, I'll be over here in the Sea of Tranquility, collecting individual motes with a pair of tweezers.

Moon Sweepers is the work of DragDrop Games, a two-person team who are now busting their chops patching the game after a surprisingly popular launch on Friday. To expand a little on the self-explanatory title, the game sees you placing depots near cleaning sites and tracking your overall progress by way of a big holographic globe back at base.

I'm not sure I have the patience to polish an entire moon, but I am certainly salivating over the delicious grey, chunky-edged plateaus left behind by the sweepers in the trailer. In general, Moon Sweepers has me thinking anew about a possible subgenre of game dedicated to cleaning up the messes left behind by players of other games. What, you really think they just "de-spawn" the corpses in Counter-Strike? Nonsense! Somebody has to come in and tidy all that shit up, surely.

Moon Sweepers has multiplayer support for up to 16, and you can seemingly spend a whole session doing low-G flips in a curiously municipal Apollo buggy... if you're an absolute disgrace to the profession. Mind you, even your starry-eyed Evil Knievel impressions will scrape away moonpowder. There is ultimately no escape from your role as lunar janitor.

I just pray for whoever appoints themselves manager of a full 16 player moonsweeping operation. At least there are no enemies to worry about - just lashings of aeons-old asteroid powder. No, you cannot lie in the stuff and make moondust angels, which seems a ghastly oversight. Read more on Steam.

#4079. Xbox Set A New Record For Game Releases In October, With Extremely Impressive Support For Play Anywhere

It's no secret that a whole bunch of new releases have been moving their release dates from November back to September and October in recent months, and it's actually resulted in a new record being set for Series X and S in 2026.

As shared by the folks behind the Xbox news for Koreans account on social media, there were 208 games released across Xbox Series X and S (and Xbox One in some cases) in October 2026, which represents the "peak month" for this year. September is second with 187 releases, and April is third with 169 releases.

Of those 208 games last month, 45% were Xbox Play Anywhere enabled, which is a pretty incredible percentage!

As you can see, the Play Anywhere percentage has been as high as 50% in 2026, and it's raised quite considerably compared to the figures we were seeing in the first few months of the year.

This clearly indicates that Xbox is ramping up the push to get as many games as possible integrated into the programme, and we're here for it - it's always incredible to get a free PC copy on top of your Series X and S purchase!

November will be much quieter for new releases with GTA 6 hogging the spotlight of course, and December should see things slow down considerably as well. As we approach the new year though, it looks like we can expect well over 1,000 new releases on Xbox Series X|S in 2027 once again, with maybe around half of them getting Xbox Play Anywhere support along the way. Bring it on!

#4078. Skyrim's Successor Finally Re-Revealed as The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel

It's official: The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel is the full title of Bethesda's next open world RPG.

The subtitle has been announced as part of the developer's 40th anniversary celebrations. Confirmation comes via a very brief trailer at the end of the company's new video, which you can watch below.

The teaser shows sand blowing across an Elder Scroll, and it concludes with an ominous quote from Yazar, a Moth Priest (remember them from Oblivion?) in service of High Queen Iradne of Hammerfell.

It reads: "The scroll offered only a shimmer, a veil thinly lifted to my eyes. A future lost. A victory undone. Sands of time scattered by fate."

Obviously not, but the teaser and subtitle reveal nail down at least one thing: this game's going to take place in Sentinel, which is both a capital city and kingdom within Hammerfell — the home of the Redguards.

You can expect deserts, ancient ruins, and an adventure-filled coastline.

When we'll actually get to see The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel is anyone's guess at this point. Bethesda has just warned that "it’ll be some time before we’re ready to share more". The wait continues...

Developers behind The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake have confirmed speculation that the game's new art direction was inspired by puppet shows.

Nintendo dropped the first gameplay footage of the remake back in September as part of The Legend of Zelda 40th anniversary Nintendo Direct, which is where we got our first look at the game's divisive art style. Series producer Eiji Aonuma asserted "we didn't just aim for realistic graphics," but it was safe to say that it was certainly a shock, the same way the Star Fox remake's art direction was for many.

Someone with a vested interest in both series is Takaya Imamura, who designed the Star Fox crew and was the art director of The Legend of Zelda: Majora's Mask, birthing Tingle into the world. He speculated that the new art direction was influenced by puppet shows, which Shigeru Miyamoto is known to love (thanks to Star Fox). Despite being his personal opinion, this suggestion was taken as fact by many, but it turns out he was on the money.

In a new edition of Nintendo's Ask the Developer series, Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake art director Aya Shida notes that "for this game, we wanted to rebuild Hyrule as a rich, dense world that felt as though it could truly exist, while retaining the feel of the original. At the same time, we wanted its colorful and quirky characters to feel like a natural part of that world."

"To help the team understand what we were aiming for, early in development we used phrases like 'a puppet-show feel' and 'the analog feel of practical effects films' as keywords," Shida adds, confirming Imamura's speculation. She explains, "Neither puppet shows nor practical effects films reproduce reality exactly as it is," and that "We also felt that there was some overlap between these forms of expression and the distinctive nostalgia evoked by the original game."

Aonuma adds, "the current development team feels a certain sense of nostalgia" – despite some of them having never played the original – and that "their efforts to express that nostalgia led them to an analog, puppet-show-like feel." But this approach seems to have gotten the Aonuma seal of approval, as he notes, "As one of the original developers, that progression made sense to me."

#4076. "IT FLIPS UP," Fallout New Vegas modders yell after releasing a funky Pip-Boy based on cancelled entry Van Buren's design docs

The same folks are hard at work remaking Van Buren as part of a project dubbed Fallout: The New West

One of the days last week was October 23rd. It's the date in the Fallout universe when the bombs dropped and has morphed into a time for yearly community happenings plus, in Bethesda's case, usually some marketing. Sometimes, modders behind long-running projects time up standalone releases with it, as has been the case this year with the folks behind Fallout: The New West, the project aiming to make their own version of Black Isle Studios' cancelled third Fallout game. They've released a few guns inspired by the canned entry, which you may know by its codename Van Buren, but the headliner from this gear drop for New Vegas is a funky new Pip-Boy design.

According to its creators, this Lil Pip 3000 iteration of Fallout's iconic wrist-mounted computer has been recreated based on Van Buren's original design docs. Worn by inmates in Tibbets Prison, the AI overlord-run slammer that the modders have already recreated for a demo of their Van Buren remake, the Lil Pip has made its way to Mojave in the hands of an unnamed ranger who's deposited it near Nipton.

It does all the standard Pip-Boy things and should work with a host of established mods which add extra features to The Courier's fancy bracelet. Most importantly of all, thanks to custom animations, the lid flips up when you whip the device out to use it. To be clear since the modders have emphasised this in all caps, I said "IT FLIPS UP". In all seriousness, it's a cool design that departs from the general blockiness of the default Pip-Boys worn by Fallout protagonists old and new. It's perhaps heavier on children's toy vibes than its siblings, but not to the extent I'd say it looks like it couldn't survive its wearer failing to step out of the way of a rogue missile or grenade.

Alongside it, the New West lot have released a Wattz Weapon Pack. Consisting of five laser guns in the classic Fallout style, including a freshly assembled burst pistol from Van Buren, the mod also includes custom animations and add-ons to help these new energy weapons fit in seamlessly with the rest of New Vegas' arsenal. They'll even be distributed throughout the Capital Wasteland if you're running the Tale of Two Wastelands mod which mashes New Vegas and Fallout 3's worldspaces together.

If you fancy nabbing either mod, you'll need to nab a fair few requirements. The New Vegas Script Extender, JIP LN NVSE Plugin, JohnnyGuitar NVSE, and kNVSE Animation Plugin are musts for both, while the weapon pack also needs the Gun Runners’ Arsenal DLC, ShowOff xNVSE Plugin, ISControl Enabler, and Sound Extender.

Nine years ago, Matt Filer officially began work on the OpenCAGE mod tools for Alien: Isolation—following two-and-a-half years of work on prototype versions. During that time the tools have been available for anyone to use, which is part of the reason Creative Assembly's legendarily scary horror game has a variety of mods already. (Though the VR mod works differently, since it's actually enabling an unfinished mode that shipped with the game.)

OpenCAGE has finally made it to version 1.0, which can be downloaded on Steam. Filer proudly told us his mod tools have "now reached the point where you're able to implement full custom maps, missions, modes, characters, weapons, animations, sounds, models, textures, and more!"

As a demonstration of what's possible, Filer is making a Halo-themed custom map. "It features custom cinematics, enemies, weapons, all on a brand new map with a custom HUD," he said. "It has reached a point now of being able to make full total conversion mods, which has always been my end goal, so it's cool to finally be here!"

Alien: Isolation just won our scariest videogame poll, and I consider it a well-earned victory. It's one of the few games I've seen frighten even people who aren't normally bothered by horror thanks to how unpredictable and relentless the xenomorph is when pursuing you. And those dead-eyed Worker Joe robots are no slouches either.

Hopefully some creative mods will give us reason to go back to Alien: Isolation, and help tide over the wait for the upcoming Alien: Isolation 2, which is likely to be available some time in 2027.

#4074. 220,000-signatory petition to "save Mass Effect" doesn't mention BioWare, suggests giving Mass Effect 5 to somebody else

Expanse devs Owlcat join call for EA to let Mass Effect "flourish anew"

The word "BioWare" does not appear in a recent Change.org petition asking EA to "save Mass Effect", which has gained around 220,000 signatories as of writing. The nearest the petition gets is an allusion to "recent revelations" that have "cast a shadow over its future", which is a remarkably gentle way of saying that the parent company shanked the creators to balance their books, after going into historic debt.

Still, one can hardly reproach the petition organisers for not mentioning BioWare - after all, EA announced that they were closing BioWare a whole four days ago, and the funeral baked meats must coldly furnish forth the pitchdeck. There are other videogame studios, aren't there? Just get one of them to make the thing. Maybe Owlcat, developers of the Mass Effect-flavoured The Expanse: Osiris Reborn, who've shared the Change.org petition on their socials.

I'm sure the HashtagSaveMassEffect petition was written out of sincere love for an absorbingly written epic sci-fi soap opera in which a charismatic group of weirdos unpick a wonderful cosmic conspiracy. Doubtless, many recently laid-off Mass Effect devs will be touched by their enthusiasm. Doubtless, I am being a pissy old crank. Still, the officious and press-releasey, 'gamer CEO' language of the petition makes my skin crawl. It reads like it was written by three 12-year-old boys standing on each other's shoulders inside a pinstripe suit.

"The decline in dedicated resources and ambiguous development plans from Electronic Arts (EA) threaten to leave this beloved series at a standstill, jeopardizing its incredible legacy," it pines. "Fans around the globe have invested thousands of hours exploring the galaxy, forming deep connections with its multifaceted characters and compelling storylines.

"It is a franchise that has transcended the typical gamer experience, creating a community that advocates for choice, individuality, and shared adventure," the petitioners write. "The potential cessation of new developments in this universe is a devastating prospect not only for fans but for the diversity of narrative-driven games as a whole.

"Therefore, we are urgently petitioning EA to take decisive action by committing to the continued development of Mass Effect," it continues. "This commitment requires proper funding, adequate staffing, and time allocation to maintain and advance the high standards the franchise is known for. Alternatively, EA could consider licensing the Mass Effect intellectual property (IP) to another studio that shares the passion and vision to keep it alive and allow it to flourish anew."

Getting a third party to make it? I'm sure the idea has never occurred to EA, and nor has it ever occurred to them that they could get a third party to make it for cheaper. Although if the testimony of former employees is any indication, it's likely they'll just end up sitting on the unfinished Mass Effect 5 forever.

I don't think either the Change.org petitioner or the signatories are genuinely devoid of all sympathy for the BioWare devs who lost their jobs last week. I wish them the best getting the credit-sozzled chatbot-humpers up the ladder to keep developers in work, though I do have some words of advice: the execs will not be impressed by your homages to go-faster marketing terminology like "passion", "vision" and the "investment" of your leisure time. They will regard this only as proof that they've successfully mind-fucked you into thinking like them. They will applaud your language's tendency to hail products as eternal and workers as interchangeable.

Still, shying away from even mentioning BioWare, while freshly jettisoned devs air their abandoned plans for Mass Effect 5, is just kind of weird! If you have such a "deep connection" with these games, the least you can do is name the people who made them, and maybe talk a little about how things got this bad.

#4073. Xbox's New 25 Years Bundle Retails For $569.99, And Here's The Full List Of Games

It's mainly intended as a freebie for PC buyers though

Last week, you may recall that we ran a story about how Xbox was giving away 25 free games to eligible buyers of Windows 11 PCs, and that the offer was technically supposed to begin on November 2nd (but had begun slightly early).

Well, last night, the "25 Years of XBOX Bundle" suddenly appeared on the Microsoft Store with an actual price tag, meaning that even if you aren't eligible to get the games for free, you can actually buy the bundle if you really want to.

Just one problem - it's retailing for a whopping $569.99.

Its existence on the Microsoft Store also means we have the full list of included games, which is as follows:

Now, as much as there are some excellent games in the list here, it's hard to recommend paying anywhere near $569.99 for them. We reckon that's not really the point though — the bundle was created as a generous freebie for new Windows 11 PC buyers after all. It's also only available in the United States.

Should you wish to go ahead and get it anyway, you'll obviously be able to play all 25 of them on PC, while around half include the Xbox One / Series X|S versions via Play Anywhere, such as Gears of War: Reloaded and DOOM + DOOM 2.

We reckon it's only worth picking up if you fall into the "eligible" freebie bracket, which unfortunately still remains quite vague when looking at the official FAQ for the 25 years of XBOX bundle.

"Customers in the United States are eligible when they purchase and activate a qualifying new Windows PC from a participating U.S. retailer or OEM during the offer period. Eligible devices include select Windows Home PCs from participating Microsoft and OEM device lines, including qualifying handhelds. The only Windows Pro exception is a qualifying NVIDIA RTX Spark™ devices running Windows Pro. Other Windows Pro devices are not eligible. The offer is valid for qualifying purchases made between November 2, 2026, at 12:00 AM UTC and December 31, 2026, at 11:59 PM UTC, while supplies last."

We've already seen some people getting the bundle for free after buying a ROG Xbox Ally X20 in recent days, so that handheld seems to be part of the promotion, but it'd be nice if we had a proper breakdown of all the eligible devices.

Anyway, let us know what you think about this bundle in the comments down below - are you hoping to claim yours?!

#4072. South of Midnight's Director Wouldn't Have Funded It, Says Xbox's Approach Was Unsustainable

South of Midnight is the latest title from Compulsion Games, a studio that used to be under Microsoft's umbrella before it reclaimed its independence earlier this year.

It seemingly underperformed, even with ports to other platforms, including PS5, just under a year after its Xbox launch.

Now, in a new interview with Minnmax, the game's director, David Sears, has made new comments about the game and Xbox's funding at the time.

To summarise, he says that, while it was highly commendable of the company to support smaller, higher-risk titles such as South of Midnight and Double Fine's Keeper, it was ultimately unsustainable because the "infinite money" had to stop at some point.

"They were funding a lot of games," Sears says. "They were also funding a lot of studios that, you know, I was like 'well, okay, great, I guess you have infinite money, you do you, I want less. I don't want to feel the weight of the obligation of a giant budget, or an army of 600 to be responsible for. I want to make something that isn't going to bankrupt Microsoft or the games division.'"

"So on one hand, if everyone you're working with is either trying to make generational games at not a huge expense, or games that have huge or really significant contemporary commercial appeal – great, it's going to work. But when does that ever happen, right?"

Sears was "always worried" about South of Midnight suddenly losing funding, suggesting that if he was heading up Xbox, he "probably" would have done exactly that.

"I literally told people, 'Wow, this could be terrible.' Because somebody is going to say one day, 'We're closing those floodgates.' And that's going to have really traumatic results downstream."

"I mean, I wanted to make it, no doubt, right? Obviously, because we made it. Would I have turned off someone else’s money flow before South of Midnight? Yeah, because I’m not completely selfless.

"But, you know, it just seems like in hindsight at least, it was unsustainable, so of course, it was going to have a 'shocking' outcome."

While there have been no official sales figures for South of Midnight, analytical estimates from Alinea back in April 2026 had the PS5 version specifically at about 16,000 sales.

Other data, such as Steam player counts, don't paint a particularly rosy picture either, and Sears' own comments in this interview also suggest it didn't hit its mark.

For a while, Xbox was funding games of all shapes and sizes in order to fill out Game Pass, but this approach, spearheaded by former CEO Phil Spencer, doesn't seem to be in place anymore, with his replacement, Asha Sharma, making severe cuts to get the business back on track.

South of Midnight is a great game, by the way, but if even the director was doubting its commercial potential, it was clearly not going to be a big seller.

Tim Sweeney's throwing a wobbler in the supermarket

How could someone do this to you, fruit, meat, and other foods on the shelves of this shop? You've been forced, in a horrific crime against the companies responsible for you, to reveal some details about how you were produced. No, this isn't reasonable information to offer a would-be purchaser, so that they can feel more comfortable and confident in knowing what they're about to spend their hard-earned money on. It's a bat signal for the anti-battery farming hate mobs and is robbing innocent food producers of their ability to rake in cash without having to reveal some basic info about their products. This, I imagine based on recent comments he's made about Steam's requirement that games made using generative AI disclose that via a brief blurb on their store pages, is how Tim Sweeney feels every time he goes to stock up his cupboards. Since declaring that Epic are going all-in on genAI and unveiling a new vibe-coded Epic Games Launcher, the Sweens has been pro-AI posting with reckless abandon. On one hand, eeewwwwww, on the other, it's a chance for the rest of us to think about what it might be a good idea for games to disclose beyond any genAI use.

Yep, fooled you. This isn't going to be 400 words of me just clowning on Tim. Some of it definitely is that (hello, opening paragraph), but not all of it.

First of all, what the Sweens said. "Forcing developers to write a political statement to be used against them by the hate mob they’re helping organize is abhorrent," he posted late last week in response to some AI bloke declaring Steam's genAI disclosures absurd. "Age ratings tell parents what’s in a game so they can make informed decisions for their kids," Sweeney continued in the thread which developed. "These AI statements are just as partisan as mandatory political essays or forcing developers to list their voting history to drive cancel campaigns and public struggle sessions.

Age ratings tell parents what’s in a game so they can make informed decisions for their kids.These AI statements are just as partisan as mandatory political essays or forcing developers to list their voting history to drive cancel campaigns and public struggle sessions.

"There is a real economic cost to Valve’s foray into forced political disclosures. Besides taking 30%, they’re also taking a potentially even larger fraction of developers’ revenue and livelihood by undermining their business with these AI hate campaigns." The Sweens also batted away someone pointing out that Epic-owned asset marketplace Fab asks creators to disclose genAI use via tags, claiming that it being a B2B platform makes it a totally different kettle of fish, seemingly because one of those fish might sue Epic if they ended up unwittingly buying AI-generated stuff to stick in their game.

You're getting off lucky, Sweens. Imagine if studios' store pages had to disclose details like how many hours of mandatory dev overtime went into getting a game over the line, the size of their gender pay gap, or, god forbid, how much the publisher's top exec earned throughout development in comparison to the median worker or lowest ranking junior! Maybe a quick breakdown of how many of the devs weren't white dudes. None of those, on paper, would force studios to write a political essay explaining why they've done whatever they've done or why the numbers look as they do. Though, you might feel compelled to pen something if, say, you know that you're operating in a way that'll put off most of your customer base unless you're allowed to hide it.

Over eleven months after Stranger Things season 5 came to an end, fans are still holding out hope for more, as stars Finn Wolfhard and Caleb McLaughlin have been spotted shooting a mystery project together.

A video of the pair on set in Chicago, which has been doing the rounds online and has since been posted on Twitter by Stranger Things Updates, shows the two walking down the street when all of a sudden they stop dead in their tracks and look at something straight ahead. What is the thing they are staring at? We do not know, but we presume it will be edited in later on. Check out the clip below.

Finn Wolfhard and Caleb McLaughlin have been spotted filming something in Chicago. https://t.co/P2LkeEOZWPNovember 2, 2026

It should come as no surprise that the 20-second-long clip has shaken the Stranger Things fandom, with many fans wondering if the anticipated secret ninth episode is really on the way. Many believed that the ending we received was just a vision made up by Vecna, who has been leaving clues throughout the final season, and that a true finale was to follow. #4069. With Xbox cuts not done, Microsoft offer voluntary buyouts to around 60,000 workers across the company in latest attempt to get rid of staff

That's around a quarter of Microsoft’s total workforce, according to reports

Update: According to Vertical Slice and The Verge, an unspecified number of Xbox staff are among those who've been offered voluntary buyouts by Microsoft.

Staff at Microsoft continue to recieve emails they'd probably rather not be getting. After telling some the other week of plans to mandate four days in the office starting in February and presiding over multiple rounds of layoffs at their gaming division Xbox, Microsoft are now offering volutary buyouts to 60,000, roughly 25% of their overall headcount.

Business Insider report that staff in the US, Canada, India, and the UK, but that not every team within the company is on the eligibility list. There's no indication at current as to whether Xbox will be affected, with exec Matt Booty having noted when announcing September's layoffs that the division was "roughly three-quarters of the way" through efforts to get rid of 3200 staff in total. According a report last week, further Xbox cuts were being planned for this month, November and January.

"The Voluntary Exit Offer reflects an important part of how we’re evolving our approach to change: creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter," Microsoft chief people officer Amy Coleman wrote in a memo to staff. "This builds on what we learned earlier this year through the Voluntary Retirement Program.

"The Voluntary Exit Offer is new for us. We’ll learn from it. At the same time, we’ll keep helping people focus on the work that matters most, build new skills and, where it makes sense, find new opportunities across Microsoft. There is no one-size-fits-all approach for every team or every employee. These are a few of the ways we’re trying to meet different business needs while continuing to create opportunities for our own people to grow and contribute."

According to Business Insider, 9000 staff were offered buyouts in the previous voluntary retirement program Coleman mentioned, with around a third taking it.

Solidarity to Microsoft staff affected by this latest attempt to fire people into the sun, reportedly as a result of Microsoft straining to pour boatloads of money into AI data centers.

As of writing, Microsoft are still subject to a BDS movement boycott over their reported ties to the Israeli military.

#4066. The GameMaker engine series behind Undertale, Hotline Miami and Spelunky is going free for commercial use on PC

Here's some upbeat news to end the day on (unless one of the other awful people working here posts something diabolical, once I'm done) - you'll soon be able to publish games created using the latest GameMaker tools for free on PC alongside web and mobile.

Hitherto, game developers have needed a Professional license to sell or monetise GameMaker creations. That changes on 1st January 2027. You'll still need a paid license if you plan to release a GameMaker game on console, but pish posh, those things are going extinct anyway.

In case you're unfamiliar, GameMaker is a series of game creation tools that dates back around 26 years. Current developers YoYo Games – who are now owned by browser company Opera - announced that they would make the tools free for non-commercial use on PC in November 2023, bringing a rare grimace of affection to former RPS archchancellor Graham Smith's time-poisoned visage. I can only imagine his happily beaming mug right now.

GameMaker has been used by such indie noteworthies as Heart Machine (Hyper Light Drifter), Toby Fox (Undertale), Derek Yu (Spelunky, UFO 50), Vlambeer (Nuclear Throne), and Dennaton Games (Hotline Miami). And also by Graham, apparently, though I'm not sure what he was using it for. It's historically been aimed more at novice programmers (see also: Graham), with a focus on 2D visuals, though the latest incarnation, GameMaker Runtime, aims to beef up the toolset's 3D capabilities.

Community dev Ross Manthorpe detailed the change in a post on the official site, explaining the implications for people who currently have a Pro license. "Developers who currently own the Professional license will still be able to commercially distribute games made on the existing GMS2 runtime, and will additionally benefit from access to GMS2 runtime source code," he wrote. "Regardless of runtime, developers will still need an Enterprise license and to be an approved developer to be able to export to consoles. There will be no changes to existing tier pricing."

Any devs here partial to GameMaker? I've been faffing around with Twine recently, and wondering whether I dare experiment with something that supports Proper Graphics. Perhaps in a few years time, some other RPS writer will be casually roasting my efforts at GameMaking, the way I have just made fun of poor Graham. Poor Graham! *camps entrance to comments with rocket launcher*

It's hard to overstate Dan's impact over the past 27 years. From shipping Project Gotham Racing on the original XBOX in 2001 to leading the creation of Forza, founding Turn 10 Studios and appearing so many times on our E3 stage, usually making a dramatic entrance with a supercar in tow—and so much more—we owe tremendous thanks and gratitude to Dan. On behalf of both teams, I would like to thank Dan for his leadership, his support, and his partnership. I wish him well for whatever comes next.

The Verge reports that Dan Greenawalt, studio head of Forza Motorsport developer Turn 10, is planning to retire after nearly 27 years, quoting an internal memo from Trevor Williams of Playground Games. "Dan Greenawalt has decided that this is the right time for him to retire from Microsoft," Williams is reported to have said, clarifying that Greenawalt will stay on temporarily as an adviser during a changeover period.

Microsoft announced in September that it plans to merge Turn 10 and Playground, the two Forza studios, into one entity as part of the same restructure that will merge Obsidian into Bethesda and hand Halo over to Activision. Oh, and that restructure will also see another 268 employees being laid off.

Turn 10 had already been turned into a support studio for Playground's Forza Horizon following the 2023 reboot of Forza Motorsport, with former developer Fred Russell saying last year that the Motorsport series died in a prior round of cuts at Microsoft.

#4064. Boltgun 2 and Warhammer Survivors devs Auroch Digital say they're laying off 25% of their staff in now-deleted posts

Not long after releasing boomer shooter Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun II and right before Warhammer Survivors launches in November, developers Auroch Digital have unfortunately given a public statement confirming that roughly a quarter of its current staff will be laid off as part of a restructuring. What's strange — to the point that layoffs are, unfortunately, expected — is that the initial social media posts, on both LinkedIn and Twitter, have now been deleted.

In the studio's statement, posted yesterday, Auroch notes their pride in Boltgun II and Starship Troopers: Ultimate Bug War, both released this year, but "despite that creative success, the same market conditions that have challenged so many of our fellow developers have now also affected us." Apologies to the staff affected follow, with a plea "to partners and friends in the industry: if you are hiring, please consider finding a place for our staff in your studio. They have worked on everything from indie shooters to AAA [co-development], and their talent and breadth is second-to-none." The studio also confirms that post-launch development on both Boltgun II and Warhammer Survivors will continue despite the loss of staff.

This is, sadly, not an uncommon thing to report on by any means. There are layoffs every goddamn week, if not several. This is unique, though, in that in the time between the post going up yesterday and my writing of this piece, the public statements have been deleted. There's an archive of the original image posted here, as you won't find it on Auroch's Twitter or LinkedIn anymore. Even with the barrage of layoff news, I can't think of another time that a statement has been outright retracted within a day. Whether this was posted in error, too early, or some other reason I can't know of, hopefully there'll be some clarity soon and, more importantly, opportunities available for the staff affected.

RPS have reached out to Auroch Digital for comment and clarification.

#4062. Poll: Vote for Your PS5 Game of the Month (October 2026)

Ah, October, otherwise known as the month before GTA 6.

Indeed, it was an incredibly busy 31 days for new PS5 releases, following on from an equally manic September — and that's going to make this latest Game of the Month poll all the more intriguing.

October's most high profile title arguably launched just a few days ago: Phantom Blade Zero, the PS5 console exclusive that had been wowing onlookers for years with its gameplay trailers, finally arrived on the 29th.

The Chinese action game earned extremely impressive review scores, and it seems to have been a big hit with fans of the genre.

Meanwhile, Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 actually managed to deliver what many are calling the series' best campaign in years, and Castlevania: Belmont's Curse revived Konami's iconic franchise in some style.

Other standouts included the eye-watering Star Wars: Galactic Racer — a fantastic racer that's gone down far better than anyone thought it would — and Final Fantasy Resonance, which turned out to be a brilliant callback to the property's traditional JRPG roots.

Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve deserves a shoutout too; another super highly rated release, and quite possibly the most engaging Ace Combat game of the series' modern era.

Then you've got the more divisive stuff that some of you are bound to vote for: both Stupid Never Dies and Hellraiser: Revival struggled to capture the hearts of critics, but they're the kind of games where if you enjoy them, you probably really enjoy them.

But as always, only one of these titles can be crowned Game of the Month. Before we get to the all-important vote, though, here's a quick recap of our 2026 winners so far...

Now then, what was your PS5 Game of the Month for October 2026? Cast your decisive vote in our poll, and then explain yourself in the comments section below.

Voting closes on Thursday the 5th November 2026 at 00:00 BST.

The state of affairs at Xbox right now is pretty grim. Microsoft's games division is letting go of a total of 3,200 jobs after years of declining financial returns. In discussing this, a lead developer for one of the brand's exclusives last year mentions that he probably wouldn't have funded his own game given where things were at.

Chatting to MinnMax, David Sears, the co-director of South of Midnight, went into where his reluctance would come from. "I literally told people, I was like, 'Yeah, wow, this could be terrible,'" he says.

"Because somebody is going to say one day, the money tap, we're closing those floodgates and that's going to have really traumatic results downstream," he adds. When asked to clarify if he's implying he wouldn't have gotten as behind South of Midnight as Xbox did, he makes it clear that is where he's at.

"Yeah. I mean, I wanted to make it, no doubt, right?" he continues. "Would I have turned off someone else's money flow before South Midnight? Yeah, because I'm not completely selfless."

That's a big statement to make about your own game, but I can understand his perspective. Xbox has clearly been in a difficult position for a while now, and you could probably highlight a bunch of games that were riskier to fund than perhaps necessary. It sure seems like a lot of people have learned the hard way that the money well wasn't as deep as anyone thought, which has led to the current cutbacks.

"It just seems like, in hindsight at least, it was unsustainable," Sears adds. "So, of course, it was going to have a shocking outcome." Hindsight is always 20/20, and at least South of Midnight exists as a result.

I've played about 50+ hours of the World of Warcraft: Forever beta, and wouldn't you know it, I'm going to be playing a lot more when it comes out November 4.

Earlier this week, Kris Zierhut, principal game designer on World of Warcraft: Forever, said that the game would have a release schedule that's a "little more laid back". Rather than the blisteringly fast eight to 10 week schedule of Season of Discovery, Forever'll aim to release major updates once every four months or so.

This is honestly music to my ears—I've been impressed by retail WoW's blistering pace and its seasonal structure, even if there have been some rocky, bug-filled patches in the past; and it's certainly something I've praised before, especially in contrast to other certain MMOs that have been coming to a standstill.

But I've been playing WoW… well, for a long time, but I've had a consistent sub since Dragonflight, and I've been able to see the arc of Blizzard whipping up its schedule into a proper roadmap. Which did pull the game back from the brink, true, but three expansions in and I'm just sort of exhausted.

There's always some new bar to fill, some new doohickey to collect, some new reputation track to chew on, and it all moves so fast that if I, say, have an off-week to go play another game, I feel pretty lost. While Midnight does major patches at roughly the same release tempo (12.0.0 came out in January, 12.1.0 came out in August) it also has a ton of interim stuff to flood out your schedule every three months, rather than four.

Launch was already crammed with stuff—a raid tier, delves, the new prey system, housing, and so on. Just under three months passed since launch, and wham, suddenly we've got Void Assaults! Ritual Sites! The Omnium Folio! Whatever Abyss Anglers is, I never checked, which is kinda the problem! Just over a month later, and there's a new raid and a new system plugged into Void Assaults (which I'm literally just now finding out about, I completely missed it). Two months later, and it's 12.1.0, which I hadn't even sat down to properly play before Labyrinths became a thing.

The idea of smaller, chiller patches in an overall slower-paced game (here's fellow PCG writer Lincoln Carpenter's treatise on the virtues of hitting a scorpion with a club for 38 seconds) sounds like a nice, soothing bath after an overstimulating day at the circus.

I do feel that prickling sense of overstimulation fear return when Zierhut talks about the interim stuff, however:

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

"And then one nuance on that is: We do plan on making content that unlocks in between … you want to stagger out some content across those four months. It's not just patch day comes [around], here's a content fire hose, and now we're silent for four months. A lot of that is, hey, there's a time event calendar that gradually unlocks things and opens them up over those four months to give things a little bit more life instead of that all at once effect."

Still, given Forever's meant to be a horizontally-progressing game that doesn't have expansions (we'll need to see how that pans out), I might find these little tasks a lot more soothing than the looming feeling I have with WoW, where at any point it might suddenly become too late to get stuck into a season.

Ideally, these mid-patch trickles will be optional tasks I can get around to basically whenever, rather than something I feel pressured to get done just so I can stay up-to-date for whatever flashy system's trundling down the pipeline next. Hit me with that lo-fi update cadence, I'm ready for it.

#4059. "Mass Effect was my ultimate white whale": Journey composer shares 20 minutes of music created during talks to work on BioWare's recently cancelled RPG

"It's been hard to see dear friends lose their jobs, and this beloved franchise seemingly vanish forever"

The gradual drip of details about and glimpses at what BioWare were looking to cook up with the cancelled Mass Effect 5 continues, this time thanks to a composer who was in talks to come aboard to put together the RPG's soundtrack. Said songsmith, Austin Wintory, has opted to share around 20 minutes of tunes he put together just as an attempt to explore where he might take things if he did end up being hired to score Commander Shepard's next adventure. Naturally, with BioWare's closure, that hasn't come to pass.

The eight tracks in the YouTube video Wintory, whose compositions have graced the likes of Journey and Assassin's Creed Syndicate, has put together range from a main theme, to intense battle tunes, and the sorts of 'ooh, there's something happening' songs that usually accompany key story moments. The opener, dubbed The Legacy of Shepard, blends pensive piano tinkling with bombastic sci-fi swells. The final track's a funkier remixed version of it. I think my favorite might be track seven, Forever Calibrating, just because it's the sort of relaxed and atmospheric backing tune I tend to put on for ambience while working.

"Working on Mass Effect 5 was my career's biggest dream project, my white whale," Wintory wrote in the video's description. "It is my favorite franchise of all time, and for the last couple years I'd been in serious conversations with BioWare and EA to jump in. My suggestion was to treat the original game's masterful Jack Wall/Sam Hulick score as a starting point, and to build on it from there with deeper use of physical, analog synths and a more tightly interwoven use of the orchestra. But a love letter first and foremost (not unlike my approach to the Aliens franchise with Fireteam Elite).

"As part of the ongoing dialogue, I decided last year (2025) to surprise the folks with an elaborate production: nearly 20 minutes of music, fully recorded and produced with synths, vocals and a large orchestra here in LA. I'd not yet learned any narrative details of what they were planning so this was just pure musical exploration. Receiving the news alongside everyone else that EA had decided to not only cancel the project but shutdown BioWare entirely was a deeply felt loss. It's been hard to see dear friends lose their jobs, and this beloved franchise seemingly vanish forever."

The composer closed by thanking BioWare and EA's music department for giving him the chance to put together these experimental Mass Effect tracks.

While this outpouring of info about what BioWare were up to with Mass Effect 5 is likely all we'll ever get of it, given the folks who were working on it have been scattered to the winds, some fans of the series have begun petitioning for Shep's space adventures not to end up rotting in EA's big shed of disused game IP. Though, surprisingly, they appear not to be teaming that call with the assertion that it should ideally be the same devs who were working on the series prior to BioWare's closure that get first dibs on any opportunity to carry on making Mass Effects.

#4058. Gears Of War: E-Day Revives Classic Versus Mode For 20th Anniversary Celebration

Horde Siege also gets a new limited time mission

After a relatively quiet few weeks for Gears of War: E-Day, The Coalition has just dropped its 20th Anniversary celebration update, reviving a classic Versus mode alongside a new limited time mission for Horde Siege.

Guardian is the Versus mode in question, which has featured in almost every Gears title since Gears of War 2. It's no surprise, then, that the classic mode is getting some love from E-Day. For those who've never played Guardian before, each team starts a round with a 'leader', and it only ends once one leader is dead.

It was a decent mode back in the day, but only if your leader isn't a silly-sausage by getting themselves killed immediately. I'm just glad to see it add more variety to E-Day's Versus suite.

In addition to the returning mode, Horde Siege is getting a new "For the Queen" mission. The limited time mission disabled resupplies at caches littered throughout the map, meaning you'll have to rely on what you go in with, and what you can repurpose from grub corpses.

We've also spotted a few additional 'Anniversary' challenges, skins, banners, and poses in the store too.

#4057. Control Resonant Is Remedy's Fastest Selling Game Ever, Led to a Massive Boost in Revenue

Publisher and developer Remedy Entertainment recently released its latest game, Control Resonant, and it's been a big success so far.

In fact, it's the fastest-selling game ever for the company, reaching 1 million copies sold just three weeks after launch.

As a result, Remedy has enjoyed a very strong third quarter, as outlined in its latest financial report.

Essentially, the launch of Control Resonant meant the company's Q3 — from July to September 2026 — saw a big year-on-year jump in revenue, up 226 per cent.

Operating profit also dramatically increased; Remedy reports €0.6 million, a significant boost from the €16.4 million loss it reported for the same period last year.

The company says the US is the game's largest market on both PC and consoles, accounting for "nearly half" of all sales.

It also says that nearly half of all players are "new to Control", suggesting the audience for the series has expanded substantially with the arrival of Resonant.

By all accounts, it seems the game has done very well for Remedy, then. We really liked the game in our review, as did many other critics, and it sounds like it's doing well commercially too.

"The number of downloads and purchases has *not* doubled."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It seems it isn't just Steam that's being flooded with AI slop. Indie games storefront itch.io has reported that the number of new game pages being created per day on the site has doubled in the past two months, and just like Valve's much bigger distribution service, the finger is being pointed at AI.

Over on Bluesky, itch.io shared an image of a bar chart labelled "game events". The chart shows that, between August 3 and October 30, the number of new game pages being created per day has risen from around 3,000 to regularly surpassing 6,000. It's a ratio that more or less matches the increase in Steam demos showcased at the most recent Next Fest, which rose from around 4,000 to over 8,000.

While Itch doesn't explicitly point the finger at AI as the cause, it heavily infers it. When Bluesky user Tommy's Homemade Games asked "Do you know why?" Itch responded "take a guess" followed by emojis of a crying face and a robot. Another Bluesky account, BardZaku, asked "is it AI dreck?" to which the account replied with an emoji of a face with bags under its eyes.

The rapid uptick in Itch pages also coincides with the launch of Claude Opus 5, which arrived on July 24. The latest iteration of Anthropic's LLM—which is now at version 5.5—has proved particularly adept at reverse engineering code. This has had a bunch of knock-on effects in various areas of game development, ranging from much faster decompilations of old games, to Steam being flooded with AI slop, and developers cancelling public demos out of concerns their games will be cloned.

Anthropic has since updated Claude to reign in its ability to directly copy games, but it's currently hard to tell whether it has stemmed the broader flow of AI generated games. Indeed, it's worth pointing out that AI Generated games now comprise a good portion of the pages listed on Itch. Out of 1,769,316 listed on Itch at the time of writing, 131,929 are tagged as AI Generated, approximately 7.5% of the total. That's a lot, considering how long AI coding tools have been around.

But to play devil's advocate, Itch is a storefront that allows AI games, and if people are downloading and enjoying these games, then adding them to the store is fair enough, right? Well, Itch also points out that, although the number of games appearing on Itch per day has doubled, "the number of downloads and purchases has *not* doubled". This suggests these AI games are clogging up the site for nobody's benefit, not even the people 'making' them.

The question, then, is what's to be done about all this? The replies to Itch's initial post are filled with calls to ban AI generated games from the store. But as pointed out by AI researcher Mike Cook, simply banning these games is unlikely to solve the problem.

From the creators of Edge: A free weekly videogame industry newsletter, featuring in-depth news, expert analysis and exclusive interviews

"I think that would be a good move. But it won't change this graph, unfortunately," Cook wrote on Bluesky. "You need a team of people to enforce it, or a very dicey public reporting system. Even then, it's a lot harder to detect than people think." Valve has also cast doubt on the efficacy of a ban on AI coding tools for games released on Steam, though its opinion is heavily influenced by the company's laissez-faire approach to operating its storefront.

Another possibility is to simply let this trend play out. There is a viral element to the ongoing surge in AI generated games, as people post their vibe-coded works online for attention and social media clout. But Itch's statement suggests that people aren't properly engaging with most of the games being uploaded.

Hence, it's possible that the people behind these games may eventually lose interest, moving on to whatever attention-grabbing scheme big tech facilitates next. The risk, of course, is that the audience also loses interest in what these storefronts offer before that happens. After all, nobody wants to wade through a tsunami of slop to get to the games they want to play.

#4055. Steam Frame kernel updated with external CD-ROM drive compatibility just one day after a user asked Valve for it

Even with the importance of physical media ownership in the current era of digital product ephemera, it's often unlikely your PC will actually be able to play the CDs, DVDs or Blu-Rays you have around the house. Internal disc drives aren't common amongst desktops or even laptops anymore, so your only recourse is often an external drive.

One Steam Frame user was hoping to connect his own detachable disc drive to watch movies and play Need For Speed Carbon (valid!) using the headset, which can run both VR and 'flat' games without a separate PC, but found that the Frame lacked the drivers to read a disc. In a very earnest community post, user Aiodensghost lamented that this fact "KILLED MY ABILITY TO INSTALL MY ABANDONWARE FROM 2006. You don't sell NFS Carbon anymore (fuck you very much EA) [...] May I PLEASE have the ability to use an optical drive?" So polite!

A Valve employee by the username gaberowe would respond a day later, simply saying "we will look into this thanks for alerting us". Around ten minutes pass, and the 'deckard-linux-no-oopsies' GitHub repository (yes, it's really called that), which is the Linux kernel sources used in SteamOS for the Steam Frame, sees a commit from Rowe that effectively turns on CD-ROM support. More savvy Steam Frame users can hypothetically install the updated kernel themselves, as this commit enabled an existing Linux kernel feature, but it's likely that this support will simply be added in an upcoming software update.

In a news role where I am continually reporting on generative AI and layoffs, it's nice to report on something that boils down to 'software developer does something cool, quickly.' And, hey, Aiodensghost can play Need For Speed Carbon despite EA, which is always a gift.

#4052. Life is Strange makers Don't Nod face layoffs and possible insolvency, French workers union STJV state

Le Syndicat des Travailleureuses du Jeu Vidéo, a French game workers union, have released a statement detailing the current status of Don't Nod, the studio behind Life is Strange and Lost Records: Bloom and Rage. The studio's fate has been precarious for some time, but STJV now say that the studio has announced ("to financial press before the employees, as has been its MO") that it is under a "safeguard procedure" to avoid complete insolvency due to an inability to pay off its debts.

The studio's CEO, Oskar Guilbert, told employees that "a safeguarding process is an act of anticipation", in reference to the fact that last year, the CSE (employee representatives) were presented with two outcomes: either future games would find funding and staff would still be laid off, or no funding would be acquired, and the company would be liquidated. It seems the latter is now likely to come to pass, as STJV state that the company does not even have the funds to complete its pre-existing redundancies plan for laid-off employees. The union also note that "the CEO finished his address with empty remarks on how much attention was paid to employees, which everyone knows was bullshit and probably written by ChatGPT."

The statement goes on to clarify that the company will be unable to complete the last remaining project that was in development, referred to as P14. This is due to a huge incoming swathe of layoffs, which include "nearly all of the non-managerial jobs":

"6/6 animators, 3/3 character artists, 3/3 concept artists, 8/10 environmental artists, 2/3 sound designers, 4/8 game designers, 3/5 level designers, 6/6 associate producers, 18/22 programmers, 3/5 QA testers, 2/3 devops, 3/4 HR…

"Management is extremely clearly going for heavily individualized targeting and hasn’t been shy about their intent to keep selected people in rather than jobs, which is illegal."

In an apparent attempt to keep the studio running despite obliterating its staff, "management is betting its all on outsourcing", expecting managers to be able to keep things moving as normal despite the alleged shift to outsourcing and contractors taking on the existing work of fired staff. STJV put it better than I could: "Anyone with a little experience with video games production and sanity understands how out-of-touch such a plan is. The costs of outsourcing a project that was mostly internal up until now and the loss of the experience gained all throughout production seem to have been ignored in favour of short-term penny-pinching with unclear upsides."

The article closes by claiming that the CSE's negotiations with Don't Nod were essentially a farce, as the company had no intent of negotiating in the first place; "Management declares that it cannot offer anything: it’ll be the strict legal minimum and you’ll be glad for it." Concerns regarding the future of the studio have seemingly been made clear by the CSE for years, reportedly living with a sword of Damocles over their heads due to repeated mismanagement, miscommunication and gaslighting, but the future looks bleak. "They ignored the CSE, middle managers, the STJV, financial auditors, all because they believed unyieldingly that a miracle would come and they’d find funds for a game that was too big, too ambitious and ultimately too expensive."

The CSE consultation will reach its end on November 3rd, following which "the regional agency for employment and industry will have 21 days to decide on the plan, and if it is accepted, people could get their firing letters on November 25th." Though, if it is rejected, management would have to figure out a way forward other than insolvency, "because, as you might have gathered, planning for contingencies isn’t their forte."

#4051. Helldivers 2's Ever-Changing Universe Evolves Again with New Venomous Terminids

One of the best things about Helldivers 2 is its shifting warfront across the shared online galaxy.

Developer Arrowhead has been able to constantly update the game with new missions, narrative beats, and features in this sort of "live" scenario, reacting to how players are doing and shifting the balance to keep things constantly engaging.

It's a really cool aspect of the game, and the latest addition is a dangerous new strain of Terminids.

As detailed on the PS Blog, these new bugs are venomous, and are burrowing beneath the surface, creating highly toxic new cave systems on various planets.

These Terminids move faster, but are more fragile than the regular species. The advice is to use powerful but less precise weaponry, such as shotguns, flamethrowers, and grenades to deal with them quickly.

If you let them attack you, you'll be poisoned. Light poison steadily chips away at your health, while heavy poison stacks over time.

Again, I think it's pretty cool how the game is able to change things up like this. I reckon it's a big reason why Helldivers 2 took off and continues to be popular.

Anyway, will you be blasting these new Terminids in Helldivers 2? Tell us in the comments section below.

Chronicles: Medieval is an impressive looking open-world sandbox where players explore a dynamic Medieval world and fight in massive, authentic battles. It's been in development for more than four years and is due to launch into Steam early access early in 2027.

However, there is a very real chance this will no longer happen, as developer Raw Power Games suddenly faces closure after funding for its game was pulled.

On Friday, Raw Power Games posted a statement to Steam and on social media channels (via IGN), explaining how the studio has suddenly found itself in dire straits. "Due to circumstances outside our control, the necessary funding for Raw Power Games is no longer in place," the studio wrote. "Without it, we can't keep building Chronicles: Medieval, and right now the studio is at real risk of closing."

This appears to be a sudden development. Through October, the studio had been posting regular development updates, including an incredibly detailed deep dive on Medieval coats of arms and how they would appear in the game. None of it suggested a studio that's in trouble, so it seems this has caught Raw Power off guard.

By the sounds of it, Chronicles: Medieval isn't all that far away from being done, either. Or at least ready for its planned alpha launch: "What makes it hurt is how close we are. Early access is within reach," Raw Power Games writes in its statement. "The world we've been building for years is finally starting to feel alive, and we have so much we've been thrilled to show you."

Chronicles: Medieval first appeared on our radar last year, not without some controversy. At the time, Raw Power Games was super excited about using generative AI for its games. Not only was the studio using Midjourney to generate (terrible) concept art, but company COO Jakob Rasmussen told Danish newspaper Ingeniøren that genAI was "at the core of our vision", adding that "When the technology is ready—and perhaps a little sooner—we'll be willing to stick our necks out and put it into the game."

Yet the company quickly changed its tune on this point, with CTO Caspar Strandbygaard telling PC Gamer that Chronicles: Medieval was "100% handcrafted with no use of generative AI." Strandbygaard admitted that Raw Power was still "curious" about the technology, but regarding Chronicles specifically, he stressed that "every asset in the game is built by our extremely talented team of passionate developers. It is not generated by AI."

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

While the situation seems grim for Raw Power, the studio says that it is "not going down without a fight" and has urged fans of the game to "keep Chronicles: Medieval on your wishlist and keep talking about it." How much road Raw Power has remaining before it's forced to close isn't clear. But since the game is allegedly close to being in a releasable state, it may be able to secure new funding relatively soon.
