#4017. Part idle game, part automation game, Moon Sweepers exploits the sickness in me that adores both Satisfactory and Cookie Clicker

In space, no one can hear you have an existential crisis

When Edwin talked about Moon Sweepers yesterday he focused on the artisanal approach to space rock cleaning. Like the puritan he is, he wants to wipe away all the dust on the moon using a toothbrush. He says you should take pride in your work, stick one spacesuit-clad middle finger up to the machines and say 'Fuck off, robots. Let me show you my art!" as you get down on all fours and brush away moon dust.

I mean, sure, when I first created a new game in Moon Sweepers, I painted with my toothbrush:

But then I got down to the serious business of trying to clean up the dusty moon, section by section and all thoughts of art left my head.

When you first begin Moon Sweepers, you're faced with an entire planetoid broken down into hexagonal tiles, each deep with dust and needing a brushing. The first sectors you'll clean take an age to clear. The toothbrush only carves a thin groove into the dirt and the tile is comparatively vast. Your backpack fills with hoovered up dust as you clean and when it's filled you need to head back to base to sell it off. Each kilo sold nets you a single dollar, but with that cash you can buy improved tools, swapping your toothbrush for a hand brush, and eventually for a broom.

It was only after I bought my broom I realised – too late to save myself – that I was playing an incremental game.

Moon Sweepers is an incremental game. There are sectors of dusty moon as far as the eye can see. The tools you start with a small, but they grow in potency, with increasingly large brooms that can be upgraded with wider brush heads and larger backpacks, meaning you can collect moon matter for longer before heading back to base to cash it in. But Moon Sweepers is also an automation game, and it's only when I clocked that that I realised I was truly done for.

Once you buy a hammer from your base's shop, you can start building conveyor belts, space dust processing plants, and robot vacuums. Stretch a conveyor out from your base to one of the sectors of the moon you're clearing and you can dump filled dust canisters on the belt instead of heading home to sell it. The conveyor whisks away the dust-filled tube and sells it for you, letting you spend longer in the fields scrubbing. Pour dust into a processing plant and it will compact it into a more valuable resource, earning you extra cash for your labour. And, well, robot vacuum cleaners look like NASA-branded Roombas. They clear the dust from a wide grid around their docking station.

Moon Sweepers, this incremental game in Satisfactory's clothing, now has me thinking I can genuinely clean the entire moon. I've abandoned Edwin's artful approach to the task and I am all in on using the robots, conveyor belts, and moon rovers to complete the job. I somehow believe this even though I have only so far cleaned 19 sectors and, according to the handbook, there are 163,842 in total. I believe this despite Steam reviews from players with many more hours under their belts shouting to me that this is a futile task. "We are 10 hours in and we are already maxed out on all the latest tools and vehicles and we are not even 1% done with cleaning," writes Marten. "20 hours played, just reached 1% of surface cleared," says Bim Fimberdim. "After 26 Hours I cleared 1.6% of the moon," writes Amigos_Of_Bako.

Maybe it's the ease and definition of progress, which is so unlike life. The irony of getting this fixated on Moon Sweepers is that I'm currently doing a lot of DIY in my flat and, despite resembling the manual labour in some of these games, it has none of the simplicity.

I went into this past weekend meaning to end it with a painted living room with some new alive bookshelves. I had to measure the alcove for some shelves, drill the holes for the brackets, cut the shelves to size, clean everything up, and then paint the living room. Yet, at the end of the weekend, I had fewer shelves and less paint on the walls than when I started. Delay after delay, complication after complication, and setback after setback meant that progress was slow and, when it did game, was more like a ship tacking against the wind than a straight line. What could have been a fulfilling, satisfying task, was infuriating and stressful.

Perhaps, right now, I want to clean up the moon because sweeping all of its 163,842 sections somehow feels more attainable and realistic than fitting these bookshelves.

#4014. Leaked Mass Effect 5 trailer is being "re-scored" by one of the original trilogy's composers, so folks can get a taste of his musical vision for the game

One of the composers who contributed to the scores of the original Mass Effect trilogy has decided to re-soundtrack the Mass Effect Universe trailer which leaked following the game's cancellation and BioWare's closure. Sam Hulick's aim, aside from making this year's N7 Day a tiny bit less depressing if he can deliver as planned, is to share some of his "musical vision" for the RPG.

Hulick announced his plan on BlueSky, having already started working on a new score for the trailer "for no reason other than closure". "My plan is to release the re-scored Mass Effect Universe trailer for N7 Day," he wrote. "A little tight, since I'm a bit busy pitching for a new game, but I'll see what I can do! I don't wanna rush it, and I want it to properly represent my musical vision for MEU."

With composer Austin Wintory having recently released a collection of tunes he put together while in talks to potentially work on a proper soundtrack for what would have been the fifth Mass Effect game, Hulick's efforts will mean there are two different takes on what Universe might've sounded like out there in the wild. It's somewhat of a silver lining to the dark cloud of the game's demise. You can rightly argue that any canned game tends to be eulogised in terms that point to it having had the potential to be the best thing since sliced bread in a fashion that perhaps over-eggs the pudding a bit, but it's always interesting to learn what those who did or could have worked on such games had in mind.

Having takes on Universe's soundtrack from both Hulick and Wintory out there certainly isn't hurting anyone. The former's also offered his view on the ongoing community-driven efforts to pressure EA into not putting the series on ice, as they have the likes of Burnout in the past. "What really sucks & cannot be undone is all the folks at BioWare who lost their jobs," he wrote. "Even if EA licensed the IP, that doesn't solve anything for them. Someone with a lotta cash would have to license it AND hire the team."

Pending that sort of miracle, the likes of the trailer, these tunes, and other details ex-BioWare devs have shared about what the studio hoped to achieve with Universe are at least meaning fans aren't entirely left in the dark about the work going on during BioWare's final chapter.

#4013. Final Fantasy 14, Umamusume: Pretty Derby, and more impacted as PHP vulnerability outages hit games around the globe

Multiple games - including Final Fantasy 14 and Umamusume: Pretty Derby - have faced outages and other issues following this week's discovery of a serious PHP vulnerability.

This vulnerability could potentially result in substantial security breaches for the massive number of websites and applications built using the PHP programming language. As a result, it was advised that online services built upon it should be taken offline until a fix could be distributed and applied. Inevitably, games were caught up.

An official post made to the Final Fantasy 14 lodestone website informed users that security "enhancements" were being made to the MMO's patch servers. As a result, new logins were temporarily disabled until the updates could be completed. While logins have since been turned back on, the server back-up feature for user's save data remains offline.

Horse racing gacha game Umamusume: Pretty Derby, meanwhile, was taken offline completely. As its server-side infrastructure uses PHP, a sudden maintenance outage was put in place - though its developer assured players no exploitation of the security vulnerability had occurred. Right now, Japanese and global servers are back online, with a compensatory package of in-game currency being sent to all players.

Path of Titans, an in-beta dinosaur MMO (which sounds awesome by the way) is still down as of writing. In an announcement made to its official X account, developer Alderon Games explained the MMOand its website had been taken down for up to three days as a precautionary measure. Players were also assured no data had been compromised.

One hopes the chaos is largely over now a fix is in circulation. But even if it is, the fact that so many services all across the globe - far beyond the games industry - have rushed to protect the sanctity of their data and that of their users speaks to the seriousness of the situation. Take a moment to thank the tech heads out there who may have had to work around the clock to get this sorted.

Fire Tower has immediately jumped into my must-have pile

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When a board game claims you can learn and be playing it in just a few minutes, I get skeptical. Few can pull off that trick unless they're lighthearted party fare (which isn't a derogatory put-down, by the way), and even the best board games can take a trial-run to fully get your head around. That's why I raised an eyebrow at Fire Tower's claim you can be up and at 'em in a mere five minutes. A glance at its array of components and grid-based system also had me hitting the 'doubt' button.

But you know what? I was dead wrong. Despite looking complicated, Fire Tower is incredibly easy to understand and you can be lost in the thick of it surprisingly fast. It's not a novelty, either; there's a surprising amount of strategy powering this deceptively simple board game, and I was soon kicking myself that I hadn't tried it sooner.

In this wicked little game, you play as a lookout trying to control a forest fire. Your aim is to have the last tower standing, and you do this by redirecting the blaze toward your rivals… or stoking the flames. While there's a co-op mode with two vs. two, Fire Tower is arguably at its best as a free for all. You can get an expansion called 'Rising Flames' to spice things up too.UK: £29.99 £23 at Amazon

This is the kind of game where shit hits the fan fast. Basically, you spend each turn placing a fire token wherever the wind is blowing – north, south, east, or west. You then play one of the many cards in your hand. While some of these simply change the wind's direction or let you put out fires, quite a few are more vindictive. You can skip fire tokens across the map, add extra tokens at once, or 'explode' the blaze so that it engulfs multiple squares on the board at once. Because you're all trying to set each others' towers alight, keeping these in reserve to use at the last second is a deeply satisfying 'gotcha' moment (especially if you're worked hard to set up their downfall).

While this could be dicey if you play at a table that struggles to lose (and there's always a risk everyone gangs up on one unfortunate rival), you have plenty of tools in your arsenal to help turn the tide even if you become the victim of a pile-on. There are abilities which let you put out swathes of fire at once, for instance, or you can deploy a Hail Mary bucket of water when the blaze reaches your tower. Firebreaks also help redirect approaching flames. In much the same way, it's possible to remove firebreaks with well-timed cards or sneak around them thanks to wind changes so that anyone who feels too far ahead won't stay that way. As an example, I managed to steer clear of most fire tokens for the majority of the game – but with some clever choices from my last remaining rival, they were able to outmaneuver me and deliver a coup de grace.

Yes, its theme does sail close to the wind after the horrific forest fires so many suffered through this summer – and it could be seen as insensitive because of that, which is entirely fair. I'd add that it's totally valid if the idea turns you off. However, for what it's worth, I think the game is tastefully done and abstract enough on the whole not to make Fire Tower feel in bad taste.

Honestly, it really got its claws into me and I wish I'd tried it long before now. Fire Tower fits into a compelling niche of easy-going strategy games that can be wrapped up in under half an hour. Plus, it's straightforward yet engaging enough that I'd have no hesitance in suggesting it to family who aren't particularly into board games. It may go in my bag when we visit loved ones for Christmas, knocking some of the best family board games out of rotation…

#4010. "Creation without a creator": Pathologic 3's devs have refused to patch an invisible apple tree, and for a blissful moment, I thought they were lying to poison Google's AI

"Maybe this apple tree is trying to tell us something."

Magnificent, depressing plague colony fable Pathologic 3 has received a sizeable game update that adds some new difficulty modes, a photo feature, and some new, worryingly folkloric methods of defeating a murky embodiment of disease. Developers Ice Pick Lodge have also staunchly refused to remove an invisible apple tree, describing this apparently "famous" bug as a hallmark of a game whose "symbolic nature has almost overtaken its function as a product". This appears to be the last major update for Pathologic 3, so that invisible apple tree is staying in the game forever.

I confess, when I first read the Steam blog in question, I doubted. The thing about invisible apple trees is that they are quite easy to confuse with apple trees that are simply not there. Pathologic in general is a house of lies: as Quintin Smith (RPS in peace) put it in his legendary Butchering Pathologic trilogy, "absolutely everybody has an angle, everyone's bending the truth and trying to twist you round their fingers." Pathologic 3 especially is a purgatorial time travel story that must be continually rewritten, a crock of festering rumours enclosed by an enormous, phantom theatre. As such, I read Ice-Pick's typically professorial account of the "invisible apple tree" with intense suspicion.

"Roger Ebert, the famous film critic, once argued that video games could never be art," the devs write on Steam. "It's curious, then, that urinals and bottle racks achieved that status with hardly any struggle, thanks to Marcel Duchamp. So Myst, StarCraft, or Pathologic can't be art, but a urinal can? The distinction, perhaps, lies in function. A urinal placed in a museum stops being plumbing and becomes a symbol. A video game, on the other hand, remains a functional object. We still have to use it.

"But enough about urinals," they go on. "Let's turn to another famous work: Joseph Kosuth's One and Three Chairs. In this work, a chair is no longer simply something to sit on. Whether it's comfortable hardly matters: as a work of art, it still functions. A video game can also become a symbolic chair. But you still have to sit on it. There's a running joke that Pathologic is a great game that nobody actually plays. Somehow, it really has become something like Kosuth's symbolic chair, one nobody is obliged to sit on. Which raises a question: should we even fix Pathologic if its symbolic nature has almost overtaken its function as a product?

"Take visual bugs, for instance. Are they broken chairs you can't sit on, or artistic decisions?" Ice-Pick continue. "Consider our famous invisible apple tree. Oh, apple tree! Why are you here? What are we supposed to do with you? This is probably the most famous bug in Pathologic 3. We've received more complaints about it than almost anything else. We have to admit there were moments when we genuinely hated that tree. Are we going to fix it in this update? Perhaps not.

"After all, it's a creation of the machine," they conclude. "Somehow, the game's code produced this impossible object. And over time, our annoyance at it has begun to turn into a strange affection. Sometimes an artistic act lies not in creating something, but in the artist's decision about it. Maybe this apple tree is trying to tell us something. So the tree stays."

Aside from making me pine for a world in which, say, EA add a "hypernormalisation" slider to The Sims, or Ubisoft redefine Assassin's Creed parkour as a Situationist dérive (yes, I too have read books), the blog post filled me with confusion. I couldn't remember any invisible apple trees in Pathologic 3. I also couldn't find any English language mention of Pathologic 3's avowedly "famous" ethereal vegetation on Google or the Steam forums, save for in stories covering the game's latest update.

My weakness for talk of symbolism notwithstanding, I began to worry that Ice-Pick might be winding us up. And by "us", I specifically mean pathetic videogame reporters, hunting for a cool bug anecdote to wrap a headline around. Pathetic videogame reporters who are subject to the wiles of Google Search, which has recently become an AI-driven abomination that subsumes and rewords all knowledge while starving actual information sources of traffic.

There have been efforts to screw with Google's AI summaries, planting nonsense on Reddit and elsewhere in the hope of skewing or outright sabotaging the chatbot's datasets. Perhaps Pathologic 3's "invisible apple tree" was one such poison apple, I mused to myself, offered to Gemini in the manner of a cackling forest hag thrusting suspiciously plump and juicy fruit at cherubic village children. Associations foamed in my brain: Ice-Pick Lodge are based in Kazakhstan... where apples first grew in the wild. Breathless, I contacted Ice-Pick Lodge for a clarification, and – bah, it turns out there is an invisible apple tree in Pathologic 3, after all.

"The slightly longer story goes like this," producer Alexander Souslov told me over DM. "At some point (nobody remembers exactly when), one of our tree assets - an apple tree, to be precise - started rendering incorrectly and became invisible. The leaves were still there, but the trunk was gone. We tried to fix it, but ran into the classic game developer's dilemma: is this really important enough to spend resources on, rather than, say, making another cutscene or putting together another quest?"

Souslov says the apple tree drove him "absolutely nuts". (I feel like he could have rolled with some line about "one bad apple spoiling the barrel", but hey, I'm not one of those stuffed shirts over at Edge Magazine - I don't mind interviewees mixing their arboreal metaphors.) Eventually, however, he made peace with the exasperatingly trunkless tree. "I started thinking: wait a minute, this thing basically came into existence all by itself. Do I really have to fix it?

"And that's when I remembered Marcel Duchamp and his ideas, and suddenly I began to feel that we'd accidentally created something beautiful," Souslov went on. "Invisible trees next to the Cathedral, where time flows in different directions. There's a strange kind of beauty in that, in the very act of creation without a creator.

"So I made an executive artistic decision: we're keeping the tree, and we're officially declaring it part of the world. So no pranks involved! Just a happy accident elevated to the status of artistic intent."

With Souslov's guidance, I fired up an old Pathologic 3 save and tracked down the invisible apple tree in-game, right next to the aforesaid Cathedral. Please find a picture of the thing's spectral foliage below – poetically captured by moonlight at the dead of 1am, through a fog of in-game Apathy. I also belatedly checked Reddit, and yep, there's a paper trail, though Souslov added that the bug is inconsistent: "their whimsical behavior makes it even better as an artistic expression - the apple tree may decide it won't meet with you today."

I remain compelled by the idea of developers telling dirty great porkies in their patchnotes, if only to excite and upset games journalists who really don't have this much time to spare. Mojang used to do that thing with Herobrine, remember?

Given the escalating chatbotification of everything, I think we are entering an exhilarating new age of lying on the internet, in which deceit and doublespeak have become weapons of resistance against the algorithm. But I also just think videogames and their creators are often more fun when they are two-faced, providing there's some fundamental benevolence involved. Videogames are all about sleight of hand, and devs should take more pleasure in that. Thank you to Pathologic 3 for planting this seed.

#4009. DELIVERY MUST COMPLETE demo launches in January 2027

Publisher Top Hat Studios and developer Yoyoyollie will release a demo for cel-shaded aerial roguelike action game DELIVERY MUST COMPLETE for PC via Steam in January 2027, the companies announced.

Here is an overview of the game, via its Steam page:

DELIVERY MUST COMPLETE—Devil May Cry meets Ace Combat. a high speed Ace-like roguelike with SSSTYLE. Cut across cel-shaded, action-packed, arcade-paced dogfights as you fly, fight, and upgrade your roster of kickass planes. Every battle is massive, every location is procedural, and every fight is a spectacle—whether it’s aircraft, blimps, dragons or mechs.

Weave, destroy, dodge, and parry everything that comes your way. Earn style points and enhance your style ranking by flying like a true ace. The stage is all yours, show the enemy your moves!

Every map is procedurally generated and no two fights are alike: Weather changes, cloud cover variation, terrain anomalies, and random map events among four distinct environmental zones change the battlefield each time you play.

Make sharp turns and aggressive plays by Drifting, because angle of attack is just a suggestion to you. Boost forward and cut through clouds, leaving everything in the dust. No, it’s not your plane. You are just built different.

The destination? Right in the middle of an all-out warzone, where elite fighter squadrons from across the globe swarm the sky all united for the noble goal of glory and peace… with only you to get in their way, again and again and again.

Crashing and burning is just a temporary inconvenience for you, however: Warp tech will pull you back.

No matter how far you fly, no matter how long it takes, no matter how many elite pilots they send after you, nothing will stop you from finishing your goal.

Melvor Idle 2 has gained a subtitle: A RuneScape Adventure.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It's easy to knock old-school RPGs, especially grindfests like RuneScape, for being games where you endlessly and sometimes mindlessly make numbers go up. But Melvor Idle, which self-bills as a RuneScape-inspired idle adventure game that claims to squeeze the genre into its "purest form," leans into that—and Jagex has partnered with developer Games by Malcs to make the RuneScape connection official.

The announcement blog from Jagex reads, "Melvor Idle takes a lot of inspiration from RuneScape and you can just feel it," adding that Jagex's support (and branding) is intended to help make the game "even bigger … while Melvor Idle 2 doesn’t take place in Gielinor, we think a fan-built idle game inspired by our MMOs is more than worthy of the title."

This isn't the first time Jagex has collaborated with Games by Malcs. It became the first Melvor Idle's publisher five years ago, albeit without a branding tweak. While RuneScape has had its fair share of monetization controversies over the years (you can see just how skeptical people were of the partnership when it was first announced on Reddit), it doesn't seem like Melvor has been compromised by trouble along those lines—the announcement blog proudly proclaims the sequel will have "no microtransactions."

Beyond that, it seems like a bigger version of the familiar idle RPG with overhauled visuals and a higher level cap of 120. You might find it a bit odd that it's a "RuneScape Adventure" that doesn't take place in the MMO's setting, but I'm not sure how many people are really invested in Jagex's games for the scintillating lore and worldbuilding. If you end up feeling like a stranger in a strange land, you can always hire someone to spam "buying gf" in a chat window while you get your idle on.

#4007. "We basically rewrote the entire State of Decay game": Undead Labs spent years trying to make State of Decay 3 into a full-blown zombie apocalypse MMO

State of Decay 3 was announced with a snazzy cinematic trailer all the way back in 2020. The open-world zombie game was due to move to colder climes, where you would face undead deer and survive the frigid elements. We've since learned that the teaser bore very little resemblance to what was actually being worked on, and was pushed out the door to plump up a Microsoft showcase.

However, what the teaser also didn't reveal was that Undead Labs' ideas for the game were much larger in scope than the two survival games that came before. For several years they were trying to make State of Decay 3 into an MMO that captured the scale of a global zombie apocalypse.

In an interview with GamesIndustry.biz detailing the recent move to independence after Xbox cut the studio loose, Undead Labs CEO Philip Holt explains that the team's founder, Jeff Strain, planned to expand the series from its co-op roots into a full MMO. While Strain left the studio in 2019, his ideas remained with the small team working on the prototypes for State of Decay 3. "He always had a vision of making an MMO and the ultimate global scale of a zombie apocalypse," Holt says. "And so there was just a different set of creative objectives the team was trying to pursue at that time."

After State of Decay 3 was announced in 2020, a small team worked on developing the technology to support an MMO, while the rest of the studio continued supporting State of Decay 2. However, towards the end of 2022, Holt and the team decided to go back to a game that better resembled the scale of the first two games. "There was a pretty significant pivot creatively on State of Decay 3's development," Holt tells GI. "So I would say the game that's present today has really been built probably since '23, maybe late '22." Later in the interview saying "One of the things I learned is just how much respect I have for teams that make successful MMOs, because I've seen them swallow people whole."

It wasn't a flippant change, as it meant throwing out much of what had already been made. "We basically rewrote the entire State of Decay game, and we will not do that again," Holt says. "We have the benefit now of this pretty significant investment in software that we got to figure out how to make the most of. We hope that State of Decay 3 has a long and successful life and becomes a live and evolving game. But yeah, I think it's highly unlikely that we spend as much time on the next game as we did on State of Decay 3."

Though, it did mean that when Xbox cut ties with Undead Labs they had a project near enough to release that they've been able to find a publisher willing to fund State of Decay 3's final months of development. Still, even with that support, Undead Labs still had to lay off "a significant number" of staff.

I've a real soft spot for the state of Decay games, though I've never played them in multiplayer. For me, they were always an apocalypse I could mooch around in solo, gradually expanding my survivors' camp and making a dent in the zombie hordes that roamed across the environment. An MMO take on the same world wouldn't have appealed to my misanthropic sensibilities, but I'm interested to learn how the tech that was produced has been rolled into the current version of State of Decay 3.

Still, one day, I want to face down a zombie deer. Granted, I'll immediately run and hide, but it'd be nice to see one.

#4006. Dark visual novel PRIMA MATERIA announced for PC

Publisher Top Hat Studios and Synergia developer Radi Art have announced PRIMA MATERIA, a dark visual novel coming to PC via Steam in 2027.

Here is an overview of the game, via Top Hat Studios:

PRIMA MATERIA is a dark surreal visual novel set in a sterilized wasteland ruled by Angels, where consciousness is harvested, brewed, and sold. Mana, a Mind Digger who survives by eating minds, takes one last job: fixing a demi-angel worth keeping whole.

“I must reject morality because it serves those in power; this is a mechanical world where I am nothing but a mechanical device and so is everyone else. Everything’s real, nothing’s in your head.”

In the Concrete Sea, an endless grey wasteland beneath a sun that never sets, consciousness is a resource. Angels farm humans for it, brewing it over centuries into Prima Materia, a luminous orange liquid that can be distilled and most importantly, consumed. Mana is a Mind Digger, someone who carves psyches for a living, extracting and eating what others don’t want to carry anymore: guilt, fear, memories.

Her self-contained existence collapses with the arrival of Girin: the rebellious daughter of an ancient Angel, dropped at Mana’s door with a simple request to “fix” her, in exchange for an infinite supply of Prima Materia. Girin’s untamable nature doesn’t make things easy, but it’s what lies deep inside her mind that scares Mana. Something old and protective is waiting, something that recognizes Mana for what she is and that has no interest in letting her anywhere near Girin’s core.

What begins as a transaction quickly becomes something stranger, more intimate, and far more dangerous. Because the deeper Mana digs, the more she finds the memory of the person she was before she carved herself down to appetite and survival.

The Elder Scrolls 6 is indeed titled Sentinel, just as rumors previously predicted – and Bethesda Game Studios has picked its big 40th anniversary celebration to reveal it.Yes, that's right – nearly 15 years after Skyrim, we finally know what the next Elder Scrolls game is called: Sentinel. Todd Howard unveils the title alongside a short clip of sand (likely alluding to both the "sands of time," so to speak, and perhaps the literal sands of the Alik'r Desert, considering the whole "Sentinel" and Hammerfell thing) and an Elder Scroll, dubbing Bethesda's 40th birthday the "perfect time to tell you what The Elder Scrolls 6 is actually called."It's incredible to witness as an Elder Scrolls fan (despite how short it is, of course), as Howard himself recently told us to "just pretend we didn't didn't announce it" in regard to the sixth Elder Scrolls, stating that The Elder Scrolls 6 is still "a while" off – which, to be fair, it could very well still be, as there's no release date or window yet.

Again, we don't get too much out of the teaser in Bethesda's 40th anniversary celebration video on YouTube – but it's enough to send theories soaring here shortly, I'm sure, between the scroll, the evident setting, and the quote.Yep, a quote – from Yazar, Moth Priest of High Queen Iradne of Hammerfell: "The scroll offered only a shimer, a veil thinly lifted to my eyes. A future lost. A victory undone. Sands of time scattered by fate."Perhaps even more eye-catching than the quote itself is the date attached to it: 4E 206. In other words, just five years after the events of Skyrim where we played as the Dovahkiin (or, erm, continue to play if you're still hooked over a decade on like I am). it spurs a whole lot of questions about The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel and its mysterious premise.And, although I'm a tad disappointed that we might be playing in a post-Skyrim Tamriel (look, I want to see the Dwemer and Falmer in action, okay?), I'm thrilled we've got anything at all from Bethesda aside from the reveal trailer we saw in 2018 during that one very fateful E3 showcase.This is one of the biggest new games underway, after all – I'll take whatever I can get, Bethesda. I mean whatever, too.After 29 years, a lost Easter egg in Bethesda's forgotten Elder Scrolls spin-off has finally been uncovered

#4004. Hot Wax sets fire to the Tetris playbook with slow-burn puzzle mechanics and a dollop of eldritch menace

Over the past couple of weeks, I've been conscious of an eerie background humming and hissing. For a while I thought it was just tinnitus, brought on by one too many listens of Control's Ashtray Maze OST, but then I realised that it was actually RPS regular quasiotter whispering in my ear about Hot Wax, which launches on Steam this week after a spell of Itch.io exclusivity.

It's the new arcade puzzler from PUNKCAKE Délicieux, otherwise known for inflicting shotguns on chess and forcing the alphabet to wear trousers in the name of archaeology, somehow. Hot Wax is actually quite straightforward by PUNKCAKE standards. It's Tetris, but all the blocks are candles, and rather than filling a line on the grid to clear blocks, you have to plant unpredictably dropped flames on wicks to slowly sizzle the mass away. Relatively straightforward, yes, but fiddly in practice. Did I mention that you're doing all this in a temple, under the eye of a "not unfriendly" eldritch god?

There's still a demo for Hot Wax on Steam, with the full release due in Valve's cathedral of commerce tomorrow. I've had a go at that demo, and it has tickled my brain. You need to line up candles, wick to wick, rather than just filling gaps, as in Tetris. But you still, ideally, need to avoid gaps to slow down the filling of the screen. Once a wick is lit, it'll gradually melt the candle and leap to any other wicks it touches.

Once a candle is lit, you have to avoid smothering it by unscientifically dunking another candle on top of it, while trying to take advantage of how the melting wax alters the layout. I found this enjoyably challenging. And then there are the power-up items, acquired by sacrificing flames to the aforesaid "not unfriendly" god. These include bombs that light a bunch of wicks at once, and acorns that sprout a column-filling sapling. Not sure what they worship in this temple, exactly, other than Tetris.

There will be a bunch of modes in the full release – from basic score attack and endless play, to a mode where you have to melt several, painstakingly arranged candles with just one flame. They're also planning daily seeded challenge runs. As with PUNKCAKE stuff at large, it's a looker, with some lustrous pixel art and lots of nifty little animations. Thank you, quasiotter – this was fun! You can stop going "EEEEEEEE" in my ear now.

#4003. Smash Bros. director Masahiro Sakurai thinks gen-AI will cause a surge of unoriginal games, but says human creativity can't be replicated

Masahiro Sakurai has spoken about the pitfalls of generative AI use in game development, saying that while he believes the technology will result in a surge of unoriginal video games, human creativity - such as that shown by designers like Ico's Fumito Ueda - can't be replicated.

In an interview with Japanese news outlet Denfaminicogamer, Sakurai was asked about his time judging for the Game Designers Awards (a role he recently retired from) and his thoughts on the massive increase of game releases since the awards began. In 2010, 275 games were published on Steam, whereas more than 19,000 released this year.

"19,000 is amazing, but I think that number will increase even more from now on," Sakurai said (as translated from Japanese using Google Translate). "I'm sure of it. That's because AI will increase the number. However, I think most of them will become 'unprofitable titles'. There are too many to keep track of, and it's impossible to understand them all.

"When it comes to things created with AI... or things mass-produced with poor quality, I think most of them will simply be reproductions of systems seen in various other games. I think there are already a lot of those now."

Sakurai then spoke about a recent (and lovely) release called Librarian: Tidy Up the Arcane Library!, which challenges players to organise books on shelves, and pointed to other puzzle games with similarly simple premises, such as finding a needle in a haystack or organising a supermarket. These kinds of games, he suggested, will be very easy for AI to replicate.

We've already seen this happen, of course. Needle in a Haystack Simulator, for example - which asks players to find a needle buried among 5 million pieces of hay - went viral thanks to its absurd yet compelling premise. Following its surge in popularity, copies were quickly created, prompting Needle in a Haystack developer Studio Bitdot to plop a bright red "original" tag on its Steam artwork.

But Sakurai continued, saying generative AI may become powerful enough to replicate more complicated games, like acclaimed designer Fumito Ueda's Ico or Shadow of the Colossus. However, he emphasised that Ueda's future games will be "something that AI simply cannot replicate ... What kind of artistic style will his future works possess? That's something only he can create. I think that's where human creativity lies."

"Basically, AI refers to things that have been created so far, but it can't refer to things that haven't been created before," Sakurai elaborated. "I think this is true not only for AI, but for various kinds of creative works as well.

"I wouldn't go so far as to call them 'pioneers', but rather people who forge their own path... people who understand and can create their own unique flavour... will become increasingly important from now on. I think this is especially true in an era of mass production and low-quality goods."

Quickly made AI games have become an increasing presence in the games industry of late. Valve's current Steam Next Fest features more than double the number of demos compared to last year, due in part to the influx of 'AI slop'. Some indie developers have even pulled planned demos and playtests out of fear their games might be copied by AI before they're properly released.

When Mass Effect 3's beloved multiplayer mode was left out of the Legendary Edition, there was much wailing and gnashing of teeth. Redemption has finally come in the form of the ME3Tweaks modding team, who have spent the last three years quietly working to not only get multiplayer working, but improve it.

"It's not just a ME3MP port but rather an extensive remaster of the experience," says modder Audemus. "This includes new features like bringing forward LE's native features like controller support/HDR, overhauled UI, rebaked level lighting, upscaled/redrawn textures, upgraded shaders, improved networking/server replication, extensive bug fixes, new gameplay modes, and a stable format for future mod support and easy installation/compatibility."

They're even adding new game modes, like one called "Unified" that combines enemies from multiple factions, and letting players either join ME3Tweaks' server, or set up their own private servers.

The ME3Tweaks team are the same modders who previously revived and revised the Pinnacle Station expansion, a lost DLC for the original Mass Effect that was also left out of the Legendary Edition. They're planning to release the multiplayer mod on N7 Day, which is also when composer Sam Hulick plans to release a re-scored version of the leaked Mass Effect Universe trailer.

#4000. Subnautica 2 dev thinks early access teams should worry less about adding features that are "very ugly, incomplete, or prototype"

But acknowledges that "early access" ain't what it was

Subnautica 2 creative director Anthony Gallegos has spoken about what Unknown Worlds have learned over their many years working in Steam early access, exhorting other devs to add new features "as soon as possible" and experiment with them right under the flared nostrils of players. Damn the torpedoes, etcetera.

The original Subnautica is one of the oldest Steam early access success stories, launching in 2014 a month or so after the program went live. Many of the final version's better qualities, including the pivot to horror epitomised by the spectacle of a Reaper grabbing your submarine's face, reflect observation of players and streamers in the wilds.

"Subnautica often launched features when they were very ugly, incomplete, or prototype," Gallegos commented, as part of a group chat about early access with GamesIndustry.biz. "This gave fans a real sense of getting to see game development in progress, in a way few other studios would try, especially for a franchise as big as this."

Unknown Worlds have "cultivated a very empathetic audience through radical transparency," Gallegos continued. "We trust the audience to give us a little grace as we figure things out, and they in turn trust us to make it great in the fullness of time."

Naturally, Gallegos thinks it's vital to keep talking to players and taking their feedback on the chin. "Be honest with them and make them understand how crucial they are to the process," he went on. "Preserve your vision, but listen to them and let them help you bring the best out of your game." Early access remains "core" to the "DNA" of Unknown Worlds, as they continue with the creation of Subnautica 2, which is about to get a nourishing injection of robot frogs.

I'm writing this up mostly because I'd like to know where you all stand as regards the "very ugly, incomplete, or prototype" - which, now that I think about it, sounds like the film Sergio Leone might have made, if he'd gotten into industry documentaries rather than spaghetti westerns. My view on early access is basically that it has become the same things as live service. I'm not sure there's a meaningful division any more between labelling a game "unfinished" and the expectation that devs will keep adding stuff to any release.

Within that, though, there's a lot of diversity, as Gallegos acknowledges in the GI piece. "Early access could mean a game like ours doing long-term open development, or it could be a game three months from a 1.0 release that's effectively doing a paid beta soft launch and using the Early Access term as a way to soften player expectations," he observed.

Not everybody has been as fortunate as Unknown Worlds in persuading players to give them the benefit of the doubt. In a crowded market (GI say that 2,924 early access games have launched on Steam this year so far, citing SteamDB), newer teams may suffer from being compared to older operators like Unknown Worlds, who got involved when early access was still fresh and exotic.

Elsewhere in the GI article, Denis Dyack, CEO of Deadhaus Sonata developer Apocalypse Studios, argues that expectations are unavoidably set by the early access devs with the largest budgets, citing Subnautica 2 as an example.

Back to you, the atrocious buyer of unfinshed games: what do you expect from an early access release? What degree of wobble will you overlook? What are you happy for devs to leave out till the final version? How important is communication, really? Does it just depend totally on the game? Here is some topical music to think along to.

#3999. Flashy internal trailer for now-cancelled Mass Effect Universe appears online, following EA's closure of BioWare

An internal trailer for the cancelled Mass Effect game that was in-development at BioWare prior to its closure this week has appeared online. It's confirmed to be real, too, amid some initial suspicions it may have been an AI generated fake.

The trailer was intended for internal use, and was created for EA leadership rather than the public. It starts with a short message: "The following is in-engine footage from our small team. It uses our pre-production assets."

The trailer shows us our first (and likely only) look at Mass Effect Universe, an entirely new entry following the adventures of a new protagonist. We see them navigate the galaxy in their own ship with a new crew of various known races including a Krogan, and get into fights using guns and biotics. There's some quick cuts to a saucy romance scene, a tense standoff with weapons drawn, and a mysterious creature being researched in a big test tube. We also see a returning character from the original trilogy - Liara - make an appearance near the end of the trailer before a big bar fight kicks off.

When first released, scepticism around whether this trailer was real naturally was present given the prevalence of AI, however IGN quickly verified its validity. In addition, Bloomberg's Jason Schrier went on to corroborate the trailer's authenticity on his personal BlueSky account.

We know very little about this game aside from this trailer. According to a former BioWare employee, Mass Effect Universe would have learned from Baldur's Gate 3 and The Witcher to deliver "a level of autonomy and choice that no other game has." The game would have also seemingly "remained true" to the original trilogy.

Reactions from this trailer are bittersweet, given the reality that the 50 developers working on Mass Effect Universe have recently lost their jobs as part of EA's layoffs which impacted 400 employees across the company. "A spy thriller is such a cool concept for a re-entry to the series," wrote Reddit user Harrywilko. "Man, I'm just so sad and angry." User TerraxFormer shared similar sentiments, writing: "God this makes me even more distraught lol. I know a trailer is not an indication of how good it would have been but I was looking forward to this damn game so much."

The EA job cuts, which took place only a few months after Saudi Arabia's $55bn leveraged buyout of the company, also hit developers at Respawn, Maxis, Full Circle, EA Motive, and other EA-owned studios. While such cuts were anticipated by experts given EA's new debt obligations, the news of BioWare's closure nonetheless drew out many messages of sympathy and anger from across the industry.

It's hardly a silver lining, given we saw this unfinished trailer while we all said a sad farewell to BioWare. But at least those staff can know they were onto something that could have been great.

#3998. Phantom Blade Zero isn't even out yet, but it could be 'one of the year's breakout hits' as it shifts half a million copies on Steam alone

Chinese action game Phantom Blade Zero already appears to be outperforming massive games like Gears of War: E-Day and Control Resonant on Steam, despite still being days from release.

That's according to sales data scrutinised by Alinea Analytics head of market analysis Rhys Elliott, who posted their findings on LinkedIn. Based on Elliott's estimates, Phantom Blade Zero has already sold 500,000 copies on Steam through pre-orders, bringing in roughly $24m in revenue ahead of its launch next week. Elliott noted the figures meant Phantom Blade Zero was "outperforming" Gears of War: E-Day and Control Resonant on Steam at the time of writing, and that China is currently its top market.

Other interesting tidbits include the fact that Phantom Blade Zero has also generated a lofty 2.5m Steam wishlists. According to Elliott, 41 percent of players who've wishlisted the game have also played Black Myth Wukong, while 38 percent of them have played Elden Ring and 28 percent played Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice.

It's an impressive start for Phantom Blade Zero on PC, and Elliott goes on to say that "pre-launch signals" point to the game being popular on PS5 too. He even goes as far as to suggest it has the "potential to be one of the year's breakout single-player hits."

These figures emerge at a time China's games industry is enjoying a boom, and an increasing number of releases from Chinese developers are launching to critical and commercial success worldwide. Phantom Blade Zero has all the signs of becoming another hit it launches for PS5 and PC on 28th October.

#3997. "We are more concerned about the risks of moving too slowly": Epic get more specific about genAI use in Unreal Engine and Fortnite development

Epic Games are, dunno if you've heard, on a bit of a genAI kick at the moment. It's been tough to notice unless you listen very hard. Tim Sweeney's lips have been sealed and no reports have spewed forth.

Sark aside, to this point Epic have had far more provocative soundbites and weird marketing lingo to offer than specific detail about how they're using genAI in different parts of their business.

Responding to questioning from This Week in Videogames, Epic's executive vice president of development Marcus Wassmer's run through some of the exact tools and uses that make up the company's current deployment of the tech.

"There are a number of tools in use but probably the most obvious ones are Claude Code and Codex with their associated AI models," he said "They’re helping across a broad spectrum of development, with some particularly big recent wins being almost the complete elimination of non-deterministic cooking bugs which we’ve been fighting for a decade and an acceleration of work related to compressing shaders which both significantly reduce patch sizes. [Other wins include] a rewrite of a significant portion of the D3D12 rendering layer (which I estimated as needing three to six weeks of work for a single engineer, but the work was actually completed in about one week with a nice win on CPU time and fewer bugs), lots of help in keeping our internal test suites healthy as well as expanding those test suites for more coverage."

Wassmer went on to add that Fortnite's seen the additions of "automatic monitoring of PC stability", "automatic root cause analysis and automatic fix generation", which he claims have sped up the rectifying of long-running issues. He also noted that, engine-wise, Epic have been able to attempt "some larger architectural refactors with AI" than they previously could due to the amount of file changes required.

The dev went on to confirm that the Epic Store launcher preview released the other week isn't the only bit of vibe-coding the company have been up to, with the practice also being used in Unreal Engine development. "Yes, we are vibe-coding things," he said. "That means our engineers are no longer writing the bulk of the code, but they are still guiding the tools to get the architectural result we want. We’re not ‘one-shotting’ the engine; we’re iterating with AI to ship features developers want and keep the engine within the memory, performance, and scalability envelopes."

Wassmer also managed to fit in some justification as to why Epic see no other way forward then shoving a bunch of genAI into their development, largely parroting the typical talking point of 'everyone's going to be doing it soon and we can't possibly be seen to miss out on that gold rush for short-term speediness, baby'. "We are more concerned about the risks of moving too slowly than we are about AI skepticism," is one of the lines he actually said.

To be fair, at least Wassmer and Epic aren't hiding the fact they're embracing this stuff, as much as Timmy Sweens hates the concept of devs having to disclose their genAI use to prospective customers or users. Sometimes the desire of AI bros to shout about their use from the rooftops out of sheer marketing zeal has its positives, eh?

Atten-shun! Company Of Heroes 3's got new single-player missions inbound via a DLC set during the Allies' 1942 invasion of North Africa. You'll take charge of American forces through a campaign steeped in second world war history that's designed to test your tactical nous and ability to upgrade fighting units to come out on top.It's out on November 25th.

As is made rather obvious by its name, the DLC depicts Operation Torch, which saw the Brits and yanks work together to invade Vichy France-controlled Algeria and Morocco. There's a "dramatic campaign arc that spans the opening invasion, the defeat at Kasserine, and the final assault on Hill 609", no doubt with copious mentions of names like Eisenhower and Patton across its 15 missions.

You'll don the boots of three American soldiers who're either in command or in the thick of the action on the battlefield, with devs Relic noting that their "perspectives reflect the hardships, losses, responsibilities, and lessons learned as they are forged into the fighting force that will liberate Europe".

In between the likes of urban tank battles and stealth ops, you'll pick upgrades earned through completing objectives, ensuring your troops fight in the manner that best suits your preferred tactical slant. For example, I assume you'll be able to go all-in on artillery if all you're after is some big booms that look impressive, but might prove useless if the enemy are safely tucked away in deep cover waving their middle fingers at your boys.

"Company Of Heroes 3 is a rip-roaring return to form and then some for Relic's much loved RTS, and its stirring orchestral score will have you beating your chest and yelling hoo-rah like only the best toy soldier fantasies can," former RPS commander-in-chief Katharine wrote of COH 3 on release in 2023. More recently, current boss Julian gave roguelite spin-off Company of Heroes 3: Final Stand a go, coming out with the impression that it's a shakeup which succeded in increasing his appreciation for the series.

#3993. Half-Life 3 is back in the news again as Valve developer accidentally sort-of references it in public, reigniting hope once more

It's been 19 years since the release of Half-Life 2: Episode 2, and yet the ceaseless clamour for a Valve game with a number '3' in its title continues. And following a swell of reports suggesting Half-Life 3 isn't just real, its development is well underway, a Valve developer has gone and sent the internet a-chatter all over again by publicly, albeit accidentally, referencing its codename during a livestream.

Valve's first attempt at releasing a Half-Life game with a '3' in its name would have been the ill-fated Half-Life 2: Episode 3, which was abandoned - despite Valve previously announcing it as part of a planned trilogy - sometime around 2009. After that, the studio seemingly had a crack at making a full-blown sequel, with Valve boss Gabe Newell confirming a few years back that Half-Life 3 had been in development around 2013/2014, but was ultimately scrapped because it was built on the unfinished Source 2 engine.

Sometime in 2021, however, dataminers began to notice something interesting: repeated references to a project codenamed "HLX" in Valve-related files. Inevitably, this led to a frenzy of speculation that Valve might finally be reviving its long-anticipated first-person shooter sequel. And evidence has seemingly continued to amass over time. In 2024, for instance, Valve insider Tyler McVicker shared some of his datamined findings, claiming what he'd found pointed to a new "fully-fledged Half-Life game" - a claim coinciding with a leak from an actor likely involved in the project.

It all reached something of a crescendo when McVicker released a new video last year suggesting the rumoured Half-Life 3 was now "playable, end-to-end", and claimed it could even release before 2025 was through. Fans, meanwhile, did some sleuthing and concluded Half-Life 3 would likely launch in either November or December last year. All of this, clearly, did not come to pass, and the Half-Life 3 hype has died down a little since then. And yet here we are again, with the latest twist in the saga being a public reference to the codenamed 'HLX' by a Valve developer, albeit seemingly accidentally.

Let us jump to a recent GameSoundCon Q&A panel (promptly clipped and shared by McVicker again), in which Valve's music designer Mike Morasky spent some time discussing the audio work on the company's games. "Deadlock has their own version of HDR," Morasky explained, "HLX has its own version, and so on and so forth." Midway through the sentence, Morasky seems to taper off, as if immediately realising the error of his ways. Soon after, Valve sound designer David Feise appears to lean over and whisper "nice work", which some have understandably taken to be sarcasm.

So what does all this tell us? Not a lot, really, beyond the fact it suggests HLX is a thing (which we mostly already knew) and that it's still being worked on. Morasky's framing would, however, also suggest that whatever HLX is, it's a standalone project, and one requiring music at that. So I guess those Half-Life 3 dreams can live on for another day. The only question remaining, which will arrive first: Half-Life 3 or the heat death of the sun?

In a new Q&A vlog on his YouTube channel, Obsidian studio design director Josh Sawyer took a question about why there are so few RPGs in contemporary urban settings. Part of the problem, according to Sawyer: They're more difficult and costly to make than other RPG environments.

"One of the issues as an RPG developer that we've found⁠—at least at Obsidian and Black Isle⁠—is that, compared to a dungeon, generally speaking, a town is four times the expense per square foot, basically. Not really "square foot" but, if you have a map of a given size. If you have a dungeon that's this big, it costs X. If you have a town that's populated with people that feels realistic, that's four times as expensive.

"Obviously, that's a generalization, but that's something that is reflected in our [past] work. As we work on areas over time, when we get towards the end, we realize: 'Holy crap, we spent forever trying to do these maps.'

"For example, at the end of [Pillars of Eternity], we had to do Twin Elms. And that was, one: A big pacing landmine that a lot of people did not appreciate⁠—so, sorry about that. But also, we're back to doing very expensive content. You might ask: 'Well, what's the expense?'

"There's a high density of NPCs, a lot of characters have dialogue. They have their own⁠—maybe not super-unique appearances⁠—but there's just a lot more custom stuff that goes into setting up towns, usually. They're more expensive. Obviously you can do it, though."

Elsewhere in this section, Sawyer cited Baldur's Gate 2's Athkatla, Disco Elysium, and the recent Zero Parades as RPGs that land the plane on believable, dense urban environments⁠—though Sawyer notes that the latter two have the advantage of not needing to work in as many believable combat encounters as other RPGs.

A few others spring to mind for me: Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines, Cyberpunk 2077, and Baldur's Gate 3's version of the titular city. But all of those really highlight Sawyer's point about expense and challenge. Vampire and Cyberpunk were notoriously difficult development cycles for their respective studios. I'll always be a BG3 Act 3 defender, but it's definitely the part of the game with the most noticeable seams.

But even if they're hard to make, I love urban adventures in RPGs, whether as part or the whole of a game. Novigrad and Oxenfurt are two of my favorite parts of The Witcher 3, for example. For a real niche example of an urban RPG you should have on your radar, I highly recommend the early access Moves of the Diamond Hand.

#3990. "Why the f**k would they add a perk like that?" - Modern Warfare 4 DMZ players are up in arms over the ability to self-revive

Modern Warfare 4's DMZ extraction shooter mode has only been out for two days - and only for those who pre-ordered the game - but already players are up in arms over a particular trait that allows competitors to revive themselves after being killed.

That trait is called Possum, and is one of the many abilities players can unlock as they level up their operators. How it works is this: if the trait is active, you're given the option, once per match, to revive yourself on command when killed. Doing so places you in a Last Stand state, and you'll need to pick yourself up from this vulnerable downed position to continue playing. All together, getting back into the firefight from dead takes around 10 uninterrupted seconds. You also lose any loot you've gathered when you revive - so you're back to square one.

It goes without saying that the ability to come back to life at all in an extraction shooter is a bold addition to DMZ. There doesn't seem to be a great way to see if a dead opponent has it, meaning every player you kill could come back for revenge later in the match when your guard is down. It doesn't take long to unlock either! If you focus your operator progression solely on the Warfighter path, Possum can be unlocked in a handful of hours. As such, it's likely someone in a DMZ match will be ready to pounce. And to say Possum is proving divisive among Call of Duty players would be an understatement.

"Possum is garbage and needs to be deleted ASAP," pdmaloney94 wrote on the DMZ subreddit. This mechanic breaks DMZ in my opinion and severely takes the stakes out of [matches]. After fully killing a team we now have to babysit their corpses until we can confirm that they returned to the lobby? Who on earth thought this was a good idea to implement into an extraction shooter?"

That sentiment was mirrored by other players too. "I just clutched a 1v3 in the underground mall, go to revive my teammate before looting anyone, and the first person I killed is laying in the corner and kills me, "SkinDiesel wrote. "Why the f**k would they add a perk like that to an extraction shooter? I get the self-revives and tourniquets, but reviving yourself from death for free every single game is diabolical."

Some players pushed back, however, offering a more measured evaluation of Possum and some strategies to counter it. "Just move on and they won’t catch you because they have no loot to pursue," suggested cleppingout. Wilus82 brought up an interesting idea too: "I was reading that people were saying to put trip mines or land mines on their bodies."

Already, prominent Call of Duty YouTubers are decrying the trait. Phixate lambasted it as "completely broken", while Wynn-Gaming called Possum "crazy" - the trait drawing criticism largely due to its potential impact on team-vs-team gunfights. After all, pushing toward a team once you take down one of their members and thin out the ranks is a strategy as old as time. If that apparent numbers advantage suddenly evaporates mid-conflict, it's potentially a big deal.

My take? I hope Possum doesn't get nerfed, at least for a few weeks. Let it ride. Already we're seeing the way it's encouraging players to adopt interesting new strategies, and two days isn't nearly enough time to determine whether the trait is genuinely broken. Let the meta game settle, allow people to push it to its limits, then, if it remains a problem by December, call pest patrol on the possum.

DMZ's new trait isn't the only thing raising eyebrows, of course.. Players have been spawning in the middle of roads and immediately getting run over, which is hilarious. It'll be interesting to see what else emerges when the wider populace gains access later today.

#3989. Cyberpunk trading sim Probably Stolen is about running a kiosk in a space station full of gangs, megacorps, and secret rogue cyborgs

I will have you know this is an original Malorian Arms 3516

I have so far not been shivved, shanked, brain fried, hazed, wasted, ironed, short-circed, flat-lined or even complained at in Probably Stolen - Cyberpunk Shopkeeper Sim, but I'm sure it's just a matter of time.

In this neuromantic kiosk game from Questing Goose Studio, you're a new store owner aboard a backwater space station. Each day, you roll up the shutter and do business with a procession of shady types, ranging from janitors with unappetising beards to sexy cowled folk with Main Character tattoos. The basics are simple enough, for all the overwhelmingly menu-led presentation: buy what you can afford, according to your instinct for the wider market, sell what you can fit into the customer's budget. But things quickly get complicated.

You've got to watch out for wanted criminals, checking them against mugshots and possibly, reporting them to security. You've got to think about how your transactions shape the opinions of various factions, from revolutionaries through corpo bosses to the mob. You've got to run a magnifying glass over robot hands and cigarette packets, identifying vintage pieces and counterfeits. You've got to head out at night to scrounge stock from the dumps, preferably without getting shivved, shanked, etcetera. You've got to pay the electricity bill. You've got to shoot rogue androids in the CPU.

I've only peeked timidly over the counter of Probably Stolen, which I would cautiously characterise as Papers, Please with a lot more wheeling and dealing, but it feels like there's some decent substance here. I'm particularly intrigued by the idea of diversifying my operations beyond bog-standard checkout work.

"Start as a gunsmith, chemist, water merchant, fence, farmer, or from absolute rock bottom," the Steam page growls. "Every product line has its own profit curve and its own way of ruining you, weapons bring inspections, chemicals bring addiction, water brings liability, contraband brings raids. Some trades need heavy machinery and permits, others just a good hiding spot and a straight face. The better the margins, the worse the consequences when something goes wrong. You’re not choosing a theme for your shop, you’re choosing which kind of trouble you’re willing to monetize."

Oof! I'll use that closing line next time I interview a producer about season passes. Maybe I'll use it next time I have to pick a wallpaper pattern for my flat.

As cyberpunk fictions go, this does seem very comfortable. Your store has a cassette player with a selection of synthy music - I turned it off after 30 seconds, because the tunes were so gratingly generic. Dare I say it, cyberpunk is a "cosy" genre these days, but perhaps I just need to trade up to some classier earworms.

I also don't think much of Probably Stolen's writing, which seems clipped and flavourless, but it's getting the job done, and besides, I'm very early on in my career as a skanky pawnshop operator. I haven't even sold any toilet roll yet, and that feels like the real rite of passage. People who prefer their Netrunner 7-Elevens all 3D and hung with beautiful, beautiful birdcages might prefer the dives you get in No Law, which Julian saw recently.

#3988. Mass Effect crossover items have seemingly been removed from Battlefield 6 following EA's sudden closure of BioWare

After EA's sudden shutdown of developer BioWare, upcoming crossover items themed around Mass Effect appear to have been removed from Battlefield 6.

When Battlefield 6's Season Five dropped earlier this month, many eager fans spotted that a collection of Mass Effect items had sneakily been added to the shooter's cosmetic menus, but were still unavailable to unlock or buy. The cosmetics included a little Normandy ship charm that dangled off weapons, some weapons that wouldn't look out of place in Mass Effect's sci-fi world and a few N7 tags. (Good spot, IGN!)

DICE has quietly removed all 'Mass Effect' cosmetics from #Battlefield6 after BioWare closure. Player card backgrounds, weapon skins, weapon charms, weapon stickers, sprays, soldier patches... everything. https://t.co/8KkjOm8nX2

With N7 Day right around the corner - slated for the 7th of November, as per usual - series fans reckoned the items would serve to celebrate the series' annual tradition and perhaps herald more news of Mass Effect 5. Those hopes were short-lived, sadly - developer BioWare is no more and the next Mass Effect game has been cancelled.

Following the shock closure, all Mass Effect items have seemingly been scrubbed from Battlefield 6's menus. Players spotted their absence in no time and shared the news online.

Battlefield 6's recent Dead Space crossover event already invited lots of divided opinions, with some players upset that the widely loved horror series is stuck in limbo while EA uses it to feed its live-service machine. Perhaps pulling a similar trick with Mass Effect - by celebrating N7 Day despite the series' uncertain future - would've simply poured salt onto a freshly opened wound. Although, the cosmetics were seemingly finished and ready to go.

In its announcement memo, EA said it was "making deliberate choices to align talent and investment where we see the greatest opportunities for players and long-term growth" - hence the decision to lay off 400 workers and cut BioWare entirely. The games industry has since mourned the loss of a beloved, long-standing role-playing institution.

A former BioWare dev recently claimed Mass Effect 5 would've borrowed from Baldur's Gate 3 and The Witcher to deliver unprecedented player choice. We'll never know for sure what BioWare would've cooked up, but a leaked trailer for Mass Effect Universe gives us a taste - a small, bittersweet, neon-drenched taste.

EA itself was recently taken private by the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, Jared Kushner's private equity group Affinity Partners and Silver Lake in a $55bn leveraged buyout.

#3986. As devastating Xbox "reset" continues, Dishonored studio Arkane Lyon reportedly only has until November to find a new buyer before it's closed

After getting caught up in Xbox CEO Asha Sharma's devastating layoffs and cuts earlier this year, Arkane Lyon - the beloved immersive sim studio behind the likes of Dishonored and Deathloop - reportedly only has until November to find a buyer. If the search fails, it will be shut down.

Arkane Lyon was one of a number of first-party studios reportedly facing closure ahead of Xbox's massive "reset" in July. However, when the layoffs were officially announced - bringing confirmation that 3,200 Xbox employees will eventually lose their jobs as part of the sweeping restructuring - Microsoft revealed Psychonauts developer Double Fine, State of Decay studio Undead Labs, and South of Midnight developer Compulsion Games would go independent following negotiations.

Hellblade studio Ninja Theory is now likely to close after two acquisition deals fell through, only leaving the fate of Arkane Lyon - a studio Microsoft acquired in 2021 when it purchased ZeniMax - uncertain. At the time, Xbox said it was "beginning required consultation with its Works Council to review potential strategic options" regarding Arkane, but little has been heard since.

Now, a report by French publication Le Monde (via Google Translate) has shed additional light on the studio's fate. Speaking to the publication, Printemps Écologique and the Video Game Workers’ Union (STJV) said Xbox management had informed Arkane Lyon it was facing closure on 16th July. As Le Monde notes, however, Microsoft's plan was complicated by French law, which requires a company with more than 1,000 employees to spend three months seeking a new buyer for any operational arm it plans to close. Only then, if no buyer is found, can it be shut down.

According to Le Monde, the search - alongside a consultation process and negotiations regarding an employment protection plan - began this summer, and the deadline to find a buyer for the studio is imminent, ending on 13th November. If the closure occurs, 217 workers could lose their jobs.

However, a union representative told the publication redundancy negotiations, which seemingly include efforts to get Arkane workers redeployed to other Microsoft studios, are going "badly", and that unions are trying to buy more time in the hope of saving the studio and its jobs. Reportedly, "several forms of takeover are being considered."

In response to the report, Microsoft did not confirm or deny Arkane's proposed closure, but told Le Monde, "We continue to explore various options for Arkane as part of the ongoing French consultation process". It also said it was "keeping the Social and Economic Committee and our employees informed." Internal documents seen by the publication say "the implementation of the plan [for the total and definitive cessation of the company's operations] is scheduled to begin at the end of 2026 and is expected to continue throughout the first quarter of 2027."

Amid all this turmoil, it's unclear what might happen to Arkane Lyon's current project, Marvel's Blade. In July, Xbox insisted "none of [its] first-party publicly announced games or projects" would be cancelled as part of Sharma's cuts, suggesting Blade - which hasn't been seen since its announcement in 2023 - was safe. Earlier this year, the game was rumoured to be dead, but a follow-up report from The Verge claimed that while it was "over-budget", it was now targeting a release in 2027 after an internal delay.

Earlier this month, Sharma insisted Xbox had "started to return to growth" following the company's sweeping cuts, but reports suggest three more rounds of layoffs are still to come, possibly starting before October is through.

A total of 3,200 jobs will be cut at Xbox by the end of this fiscal year as part of an extensive restructuring. One of the casualties already is id Software, which has lost somewhere in the region of half its staff. That said, if you ask current leadership, everything at the Doom and Quake studio is fine and dandy at the moment.

Marty Stratton, studio co-director of id Software, commented on how the company's been doing since the layoffs hit over the summer during a preview event for Doom: The Dark Ages DLC. "We're doing great," he says, per IGN.

"Not to handwave the [layoffs] away," he adds. "Everybody knows we had about half of our studio exit as part of that. But there was a very deliberate effort to make sure that we were incredibly viable coming out of that across everything we do, across game development and technology department."

Being down half your team is pretty significant. Reportedly, id Tech itself, the studio's in-house engine, is now being managed by exactly one whole person. While that's certainly viable financially, I'm not sure how structurally sound that is long-term.

Stratton goes on. "We're working more closely with MachineGames than ever," he states. "We've always had a very close partnership with them, but I think we're at a point with technology development that both teams are incredibly talented and have incredibly talented engineers and we're really on an amazing path that had started pre-[layoffs]."

A question mark has loomed over MachineGames since the release of Indiana Jones and the Great Circle. The prevailing rumor is Wolfenstein 3, and given the general push toward established IP Xbox has been making amid all the redundancies, that seems a safe bet.

But what the collaboration between the two companies looks like, and where that leaves the next Doom, are bigger questions. "We'd kicked this off earlier this year. We're really excited about that," Stratton adds. "We're both really really bullish on what we have ahead."

#3984. GTA 6 has a smell reaction system, which immediately joins Red Dead Redemption 2's dynamically shrinking horse balls on Rockstar's list of immersive symbols of excess

Florida of course being full of smelly smells that smell...smelly

Any reminder of Red Dead Redemption 2's temperature sensitive horse testicles brings a smile to my face. In truth, I can't say I've ever zoomed in close enough to properly take in the spectacle of Arthur Morgan's mount having its nuts dynamically expand and contract based on whether he's riding through snowy mountains or across baking plains, but I do always get a kick out of knowing such a thing's happening as I play. To this point, the horse balls have been the most infamous or meme-worthy example of Rockstar's obsession with going all-in on realistic detail to an arguably unnecessary degree, one that borders on overindulgence which players could conceivably never notice if they weren't expressly told about it.

That philosophy's gone nowhere, so GTA 6 was always going to have a feature that'd become as much of a metaphor for excess as those beloved balls. It may well be the smell reaction system revealed in Edge's long read on the game.

According to this latest rundown of things in GTA 6 and how they were made, Rockstar devs at one point had to make a character react to a not nice smell for a specific bit of "explorable content" stuffed into the game. Cool. One person scrunching their face up to show things are getting stinky in one minigame or mission. Leave it at that.

They reportedly did not leave it at that, later going back to flesh out this one smell reaction into a broader system which other locations to inspire various degrees of face-scrunching by protagonists Lucia and Jason. Cue, in the demo of the game in action which Rockstar gave Edge, Jason walking into a house and starting to act like someone who's just walked into a shower-averse teenager's bedroom during a heatwave despite that not having been set up as part of a deliberately crafted encounter. It's horse ball-esque dynamic systems playing off each other, and voila, a man going eewwwwwwwwwwwww.

Would GTA 6 be any worse off if, as in previous entries, you weren't being shown as expressly which places the crim whose boots you're sharing finds a bit too pongy for their liking? Almost certainly not, but hey, when you've decided your business is taking the detail to levels other games could only dream of having the budget for, getting to the point where you're adding a fiftieth layer of icing to a cake so packed to the gills with different tastes and flourishes that your guests will struggle to appreciate or even notice them all unless you painstakingly point out each one is sort of inevitable.

Another layer of gold wrap on the Bugatti, another brick made of diamonds in a wall projected to be the most lucrative of all time, another farty stench in a room already drowning in foul aromas. It's beautiful in the perverse sort of way that I imagine the Palace of Versailles was to anyone who wandered its gilded halls just prior to the French revolution. To be clear, this isn't any sort of slight on the devs who'll no doubt have worked hard to bring this system and others in GTA 6 to life, a number of whom have a recoginition vote on their unionisation efforts coming up next month.

From a player perspective, one can only hope that by the time GTA 6 hits PC, the RAM crisis has led hardware makers to invest heavily in smellivision tech, so that players around the world can drink in the guffs causing their butt naked on-screen analogue's eyes to water or revel in the stink caused by hitting someone with a bag of dog shit. Forget AI bollocks, this is the future, I scream as I retch into a toilet bowl while some funky tunes from Justice play in the background.
